Oh boy, this is going to be a long one. I put Naruto Shippuden on Hiatus way back when in 2012 or so, when I caught up to the manga. At that time, Bee was first being introduced as a new character. 8 or so years later, I finally, over the stretch of a month, finally finished the entire show. There will be some spoilers in this review. It's been like 7 years since this show has been released, so I highly doubt you haven't watched this show, or plan on doing so anytime soon. In all honesty, Naruto: Shippuuden can be said to contain manyflaws, some including ridiculous plot armor, plot holes, and questionable character development. Let's go over them. When talking about the plot in Naruto, one also has to include characters. Characters become a major plot point in many of the most important arcs in Naruto, and so they have to be discussed side by side. And what else but starting with the Main Character himself, Uzumaki Naruto? 

Naruto can't be considered a terrible shounen main character, and he certainly fills the role quite well. The problem is that much of his character could have been developed in a much greater way than what actually ended up ensuing in his self reflecting and confrontational arcs. His  beginning arcs were probably one of the best I've ever seen in a show: gradually transforming from a loner to an identity as a member of team seven. Iruka was the first person to acknowledge Naruto, and this gradual dynamic between Sasuke and Naruto begin to begin. Naruto is able to get acknowledgement and satisfaction from the bonds that he painstakingly forms, and Sasuke doesn't even want to form them in the first place, and thus begins the whole entire setup for their rivalry down the path. However, somewhere along the line, Naruto begins to stagnate as a character. He's extremely immature throughout the entire show, and despite this childish nature, still manages to mature in different ways. This is confusing to say the least. When it comes to his goals, which he eventually finds out with his interactions with Jiraiya and Pain, he's able to easily find his determination and objectives. which of course, can be summed up in: peace. Yet, at the same time, he's idealistic and lacks any sort of concrete plan that allows him to follow up on that objective, and this continues until the very end of the series, where he still has this immature idealistic world view. Neji's death might have been a wake up call for himself, and in some ways, it is. He realizes that in conflict, not everyone can be saved, yet he shouldn't wallow in that despairing emotion, but make sure that the ideals that the person died for wasn't for naught. Perhaps Itachi's talk about how not every burden can be shouldered on his own could also suffice as a rare form of maturing. However, this is where his maturation as a character seems to end, and these moments are few and far between, not to mention, extremely short. There are so many characters and story arcs that focus on Naruto persevering and reinforcing his determination for his goal, but there seems to an extreme lack in any sort of maturing or learning of how he's able to complete such a task. 
Instead of learning from his own mistakes, he instead gets convenient plot armor in the form of who knows what all scattered throughout the entire series, and this makes him bypass any sort of realization that his actions have consequences. Over and over again, you see Naruto charging into battle, determined to follow through his ideals, and stubborn enough to not ever budge. This is alright, but in the end, he gets beat up, but bailed out by whatever plot devices the author wants to throw at him. Maybe, if someone got extremely hurt, someone died for his mistakes, this would have been a key to his character development. Neji's death occurred in the rare moments that Naruto's actions were completely logical and were not made in a hot blooded attempt to stop the enemy. There is no arc where he undergoes the consequences of his actions, nor is there any arc that helps him understand the reality of his dream. What exactly is it that he can do to make hate disappear from the world? This self searching arc never began. I think it would have been immensely helpful to the depth of Naruto if there was just a single arc where he sees how conflict happens and faces the reality that there isn't just a single "good" side and "bad" side. Naruto obviously understands this theme very well, but it was always through the flashbacks of other people that he watches as a bystander, and never as a personal experience, and as a result, he never truly matures as a character as intended. The fourth ninja war could have been a great example of this happening, if not for the fact that that entire arc was pretty dumb. It clearly marks the shinobi world as "the good guys" and Madara and his gang, "the bad guys." Is it really a shinobi war if it's essentially Madara versus the entire world? It's ridiculous how such a great potential arc became a "good" vs "bad" guy arc. If there was a split in nations supporting and going against Madara, this could not only have been a great way to express how conflict isn't always black and white, but also great fights. Instead, we see lame fights between reanimated people, rather than real ones with real motivations. There is such a distinction that the author wants to make that "these guys are bad and mind controlled by jutsu" that it was hard to sit through. In fact, instead of having people side with Madara, in the end, everyone that used to support him goes against him, truly making it so that there is as little need for any distinction between good and bad at all. The entire war arc feels like a "side character" arc and doesn't feel like there was any sort of real engagement or conflict of interests in place, since again, everyone on the enemy side was mind controlled or copies of Zetsu.
Sasuke, on the other hand, manages to be a much better character in this aspect. Broiled in revenge, he kills his older brother, only to find out the undertones and plots that are hidden in the village. He sets his eyes on the sole reason why Itachi had to kill his own clan: the clan itself. However hot blooded revenge is stopped short by meeting with his brother once again through edo tensei. This arc of revenge to redemption is a clear turning point in Sasuke's character, and is the reason why his goals go from a revenger to a desire to be a savior. This decision to become a savior was also only after he came face to face with the previous hokage, which again, further reinforce the fact that not everything is light and dark. He also cements his perfect idea of what it is to achieve his goal as a savior.
What Naruto and Sasuke both have in common are their idealistic hot blooded pursuits in their goals, yet Sasuke manages to comprehend, through his self reflection, on how to achieve his goals, however silly they might have been. And despite the fact that  there is such a focus on Naruto's character the entire series, there fails to be any sort of progression as a character in Naruto for the most part, only reinforcing his idealistic dreams, while Sasuke is able to become a more well rounded character with much less screen time and focus. In the end, Naruto's and Sasuke's goals are both idealisitc, but Sasuke matures more as a character, and even determines his next course of action without much difficulty, while Naruto is merely led along the plot of "defeating the bad guys" for essentially, the entire series. This does make Naruto progress as a character, but stops short of actually trying to make his abstract goals tangible through his own way of thinking.

Plot armor is also a pretty big issue for Naruto, but it is such for all shounen series in general, but the more pressing issue is power progression. Naruto is considered to be a pretty untalented person, yet he still manages to become the strongest shinobi in the world. How did that happen? Power progression in Naruto Shippuuden is one of the most inconsistent things. People get crazy powers throughout the entire show, and not only is this method fast and instantaneous, it also happens so often. There are so many times in the show where a huge fight is tilting greatly in one side's favor, but due to a crazy powerup reversal, the other side has a great advantage. Both the "good side" and "bad side" do this constantly near the end of the arcs. Not only is this pretty stupid, it doesn't make a lot of sense plot wise. There were many times where some people were so overpowering the other side that the fight was declared over, yet somehow, they don't finish them off and allow them to power up. This power progression is also reserved for a select few, so essentially Sasuke and Naruto become the only relevant characters, power wise at the end of the story. This brings more consequences other than poor plot. It completely destroys and semblance of need for any side characters, and this is my biggest problem with the series.

Naruto has one of the best cast of characters in the entire series. Lee, Tenten, Gaara, Neji, Guy, Iruka, Ino, etc etc. There are definitely quite a cast of arcs dedicated to a lot of side characters in Naruto, and it is one of the best points in Naruto. These characters have great personalities and contributed to the plot greatly, earlier in the story, yet fade to obscurity as the story goes on, and when Sasuke and Naruto become overpowering and leave everyone behind to the point where they don't become any sort of meaningful support. Arcs without Naruto in it tend to be pretty damn good. My favorite arc in Shippuuden was definitely Shikamaru and Asuma's arc. The fights were great, Shikamaru's development was great, and the enemy was interesting to watch. In the end, it goes to show that it was definitely possible for there to be a lot more potential arcs concerning the rest of the cast of characters, but it was never explored, but rather just wasted on Naruto. Fights were flashy for sure, but when the same message of "wow you're just like me, I was lonely and sad too," and "bad guys are bad, I want peace" gets repeated over and over again, you wonder what could have happened if these characters got more love. Not only are characters shoved aside because power level wise, they were completely obsolete, but it also got rid of any sort of interesting fights involving ninjutsu. Shikamaru's arc, again, is an excellent example of this. His shadow binding jutsu was used in unique and different ways, and so were the enemy's jutsu as well. He couldn't afford to get injured because the enemy was able to reflect injuries right back at you. There was a lot of strategy and matchups that were used, but in later fights, this doesn't happen. It's just more like "I'm going to bash you in with my OP power, you don't stand a chance," and for the most part, this is basically what happens. No unique techniques get introduced, no interesting strategies, but just straight up broken and OP powers get brute forced into defeating the enemy. Elemental weaknesses and strengths essentially don't get mentioned ever again at some point. It really sucks. Power creep in Naruto not only demolish characters, but it also got rid of the interesting ninjutsu's that people were employing in fights. This is most apparent in one single ability: Edo tensei. A completely busted and overpowered ability that has so much impact on the ninja war, yet apparently becomes super weak in the later arcs. What happened to invincibility? What happened to unlimited chakra? Edo tensei manages to become one the most busted jutsu's in the show, but becomes practically useless by the end of it, and it also highlights the lack of consistency. Edo tensei not only becomes obsolete because of power creep, but more importantly, it actually gets weaker for no reason at all. It goes from an invincible form  that can't be stopped other than sealing. Regardless of element type, sage chakra, or OP abilities, they will regenerate. Regardless of how much chakra is used, they can regenerate. These features become disabled right after the ninja war arc, and it's never explained. What a bunch of bull.

I talk about characters in Naruto as if there were no bad ones. Far from the truth. Sakura and Kuruma are the worst characters, by far, in the series. I always knew the meme about Sakura being useless was a thing, but I thought it was an exaggeration , if anything. It really wasn't. Sakura is a piece of emotional baggage that had literally no influence on the plot other than the fact that Naruto liked her. Liked. her. It was pretty clear that Naruto liked Sakura in the beginning of the series, but as time went on, Naruto accepted that Sakura didn't have the eyes for him, and Naruto even matures so great that he calls her out on his fake confession. This shows how much as a character Naruto grew in this department at the very least. If this were in the beginning, Naruto would have accepted it no doubt. Sakura, on the other hand, can't make up her mind. Time and time again, she can't make her own decisions, and it's clear that her only role in the series is to make us pissed at her. She can't make a decision on Sasuke. Or on killing Obito. or on her resolve to fight. She is such a static character, as she never truly progresses or matures throughout the entire series, and is babied the entire way by all the people around her, especially Naruto. She too, suffers from power creep immensely, and never manages to catch up to, even after her line of "I've caught up to them, Tsunade" quote. What a joke. She's unironically also a simp. Loves Sasuke from beginning to the end, despite Sasuke only berating her, trying to kill her, and not making a bond with her to the end. Even after all the crap Sasuke does to her, she is irrevocably in love with him. Holy. Crap. Naruto moves on with his love eventually, yet Sakura manages to never do such a thing. Without reason, no matter what Sasuke does, Sakura loves him anyway. She didn't do a single thing for Sasuke, in the end either. As Sasuke said, the only bond he had was with Naruto, not Sakura. Naruto was his only friend. Naruto is the one that Sasuke acknowledges, not Sakura. Overall, not an impactful character. She hogs a bunch of screentime only because she was on team seven in the past with Naruto and Sasuke. 
Kuruma's definitely a much better character than Sakura, but he's still a pretty bad one. He just randomly transitions from an amalgamation of evil to "good guy" within the span of a few minutes in a single episode. I think we all knew that Naruto was going to bond with Kuruma and that Kuruma was going to eventually befriend Naruto, but what a lame and anticlimatic bonding that was! Sure, there were many arcs regarding the evil nature and uncooperativeness of Kuruma, and the his tug of war with Naruto, but there really wasn't much of a bonding arc, and this was much needed. In the end, he gets defeated by Naruto, and acknowledges him as a result. You might be thinking that Sasuke's bonding with Naruto was essentially the same thing, but Sasuke wasn't actually "defeated" by Naruto physically, but philosophically. and this gets explained a lot more. Kuruma's arc felt like subdued=good guy. Not only was it short, it didn't make a lot of sense.

That concludes the main points I wanted to share. There was a lot more to cover, but these were the major points that I wanted to cover.

Side note: I had the benefit of being able to watch both the anime and read the manga long after the series had ended, and as a result, I was able to navigate any and all fillers by combining my reading through any chapters that were mixed/filler, and skipped all the episodes that were filler. As a result, I had the unadulterated canon viewing experience, and in my opinion, the best way to experience the show. I can't say I would have enjoyed the series as much if I didn't have this opportunity, and can't blame other people for disliking the show because they had to sit through all the filler content. But hear me out. I get it, the filler is bad, but unlike one piece's way of introducing filler, in Naruto, pacing is still alright. There's just filler in the form of entire filler arcs and flashbacks. This can easily be skipped. One piece's filler was "unskippable." The show was just at a constant snails pace, which led me to adopt only the manga as a result. Given I could skip the filler, I still rate the anime decently, comparable to the manga.

Naruto as a series, is an incredibly complicated masterpiece. Assuming the person reading this has first finished the original Naruto series of our blond haired hero in his trademark Orange tracksuit, I will give a quick summary of some of the critiques I have of this series and what to look forward to in this next amazing sequel. First of all, the soundtrack remains iconic and amazing. The openings remain catchy and the soundtrack is both epic and marvelous. It tends to move away from the very fast-paced Japanese sounding instrumentals of the first series and enters into hymn and choir territory, especially with relevanceto characters of God-like status relating to the plotline.

Naruto shippuden is a very lore based series, and relates more towards philosophy and morality then the first series ever did. The battles are long, the speeches are longer. I assume Creator Kishimoto wanted his viewers to age up with the anime, beginning to question things they never did as a child. Therefore, expect the anime to become very complex and confusing at some points.

Unfortunately, The loveable Konoha  side characters that we independently learned and watched fight in the Chuunin exams and Sasuke retrieval Arc have a lesser role in the sequel. New characters and plot lines are introduced and many shinobis are cast to the side lines. The sequel is very much about focusing Sasuke and Naruto's bond and Naruto's own personal character development..
 I would argue that  the young shinobis still have much relevance, but less screen time in the main storyline as it progresses.
The meme of 'NAAAAAAAAAAAAAAARUTOOOOOOO' and 'SASUUUUUUUUUUKEH' is pretty much relevant to the series as Naruto fights further to bring Sasuke back to the village. ^_^

The new characters, especially the Akatsuki characters throughout the story, are super interesting and unique, so look out for them. They are all powerful individual shinobi with incredibly unique designs and jutsus. I found them to be the most enjoyable of the series and I hope the reader does too!

Naruto Shippuden may not have the carefree, often comedic,  nostalgic attitude of the first series main storyline, but it still provides a much enjoyable series and definitely a fantastic must see sequel to the first series to finally get a sense of closure.

Sound 9/10: beautiful, the themes that play during a certain group, truly resonates their character. Openings and endings were solid. No complaints at all.

Character 10/10: This is what carried the show. This. When you talk to someone about naruto, they don't say I wanna be naruto, the say I wanna be madara,  or itachi  or daedara. The villains were so well designed and have so much personality it truly is what made naruto into a masterpiece in my opinion. Naruto didn't carry the show, the villains did. Then there's the most significant characters,  naruto and sasuke. The love/hate between them is so beautiful and eloquent, that it draws out a multitude of emotions from the watcher, who's awaiting them to meet. I've never seen such love portrayed as the way naruto did for sasuke in any anime really.

Enjoyment 8/10: Naruto is truly unique. It's an anime I can see why so many people admire it. But let's be honest here, if the villains weren't as cool as they are , I don't think it would've been a show to remember.

Okay this is going to be long so please bear with me. Prior to me many have written reviews on this so, you may not find many new points. So I will not write about separately about story, art etc instead I will try to provide my view objectively. Now coming to Naruto Shippuden, I believe it has received so much positivity majorly due to its nostalgia factor. It may not be as bad as I make it to be for some people but let me explain you in detail. First let us discuss the main protagonists of the show: The main problem I had with thisis the main trio. We can simply state them in three words ie, dumb,dumber,dumbest. Yes, they are so dumb. Naruto, the protagonist of the series never ever grows up. He is same as he was in Naruto(prequel) except for a few changes. And the people who used to dislike him come to like him for his same dumb antics. Even the characters who had rarely interacted with him believe in him and give *If its Naruto then it can be possible* vibes. They are the same people who hated him before.

The dumber part of the show goes to sakura. She is there to make us believe that she is equally strong and determined in the team #7. Her love(only if you can call it that) towards Sasuke is so unreasonable and forced. She is so clingy and is there just to make life of naruto difficult. She, like naruto never stops the "sasuke sasuke" thing which is annoying as hell. Kishimoto tries so hard to make us think she has become better. She has always been useless, only occasionally used to make us believe even she is strong. At other parts of the show ahe is just there to occupy space.

Now comes the dumbest part of the show. Yes, you guessed it right. It is none other than Sasuke. He is one of the main characters of the show but is absent for nearly half of the show. He gets ready to follow some stranger for the sake of power and ends up abandoning his comrades. To speak it was due to his jealousy towards naruto that made him to become strong. His motives are so messed up and they fluctuate tad bit too much to sympathize for his losses. Even till the end he is as hopeless as a person can get. I am trying to not spoil much but his sense of thinking is so messed up in the later part of the series.

This is not all, our main protagonist is so righteous that he goes on and on about friendship that he ends up putting all of his friends into risk in order to save one selfish, arrogant idiot. He gives so lengthy speeches to the antagonists that it makes me sick. He never stops ranting. He is just too loud and annoying for a protagonist. His attitude isn't any better as he does some pretty nonsensical shit during missions that would definitely make you question his maturity even after these many years. 

Yes, 2 years later, Naruto became 15 years old, and his personality is still the same. He is still unable to refrain from himself from doing something stupid that would fuck up his whole team. What irritates me are the techniques. For some reason, everything is an upgraded version of his previous techniques; Rasengan to Odama Rasengan to Rasenshuriken. 5 Clones to 100 Clones, then went to 1000 Clones.

Flashbacks are normal in many animes. However, Naruto is an exemption. The flashback last so long and most of the scenes are being repeated. Flashbacks in Naruto do not bear much significance in the story and yet I do not see the reason in dragging the flashbacks.

The fight scenes in this show are all talk and no battle. The fight scenes bores me to death. Fight scenes are very predictable. All characters spend most of their time just standing an telling lame stories rather than fighting. This is how the fights go- Naruto uses Kagebunshin. The enemy beats all of them, beats Naruto to pulp, then Naruto teaches the enemy about life and friendship and at last Naruto hits the enemy with a rasengan and the fight ends.

The backstories every antagonist is almost the same. Almost all were good but a single situation fucked up their lives and they end up on the bad side. This is not to say that there are no good characters. They are there but they take the back seat in the show.

It took Naruto heck lot of episodes to just get a single power up. There is nothing wrong with it but in the final few arcs he literally becomes god which makes all his hard work seem pointless.

The final arcs:
Ah! These are the worst part of the the show. It involves the great shinobi war which is dragged to death. It is very poorly written and the antagonist at the end of the show makes this show a joke. There is no build up for it. Yes it is the kaguya part. The war part almost makes naruto and his precious friend sasuke gods. They become gods to defeat gods and naruto is now even capable of healing. The final arcs make all the established rules and world building look stupid. Logic goes for a toss in most parts.

The good parts like a few arcs and characters are highly overshadowed by the terrible pacing, whole lot of filler and dumb main trio. The pacing is so terrible that there are so many pauses and others efforts put in to drag the show which make me feel nothing even after a bunch of episodes, as they cover very little progression. Don't even get me started on fillers. They just dragged the anime to make some 700 episodes which is not very enjoyable.

Finally there are good aspects which others mentioned so I chose not to as I feel they are so overshadowed by the fillers, pacing and the terrible main cast. I don't know how many people liked naruto but to me he seems too dumb and immature. So I mainly believe that this show rides on nostalgic factor. It has many notable inspirations taken from famous shonen series like HunterxHunter and Dragon Ball. 

In the end all I want to say that there are better shonen series like HunterxHunter and it is not worth the time you put into this series. Believe me when I say you won't miss a single part of story even if you watch it in 2x speed. By the way this is my first anime review. Anyway it doesn't really matter as I have rather made this review pretty late I guess.

I beg your pardon for any grammatical mistakes.

Thank you for your patience. Signing off...

This anime is incredible, one of the best ninja stories of the entire century. Something so motivating, inspiring and beautiful that is considered a classic in the world of animation. The music, visuals and characters connect with the entirety of the human soul. Yes there are flaws, yes there are filler and so on. However that does not truly determine how amazing this story is, the history, world building, storyline and the aesthetic in general is what makes it stand out. The story is set in this blend of Japanese feudalistic society mixed in with current technological innovations, the atmosphere is set in this brutalworld of war and conquest. In which there is this constant tension of war between empire like nations, in this show we get the perspective of The Hidden Leaf (Konoha).  A village superpower with a diverse range of clans with different abilities.

In this society we meet our protagonist Naruto Uzumaki, a mischievous boy who lives as an orphan. Compared to the original show in Shippuden, you can see him grow as a teenager and see how he matures and understands the harsh realities of human nature and the world. 

Simple messages are portrayed  in a complex fashion especially in the upcoming arcs, were villains are too allowed their perspective and how they came to be. At times as human beings there are plenty of life lessons and reminders that Naruto Shippuden excellently shows such as the importance of loved ones and friends, a basic concept that allows human beings to bring meaning and to flourish. Secondly the importance of hatred and how traumatic events can haunt one forever, as we see in Saskue Uchiha

From the characters each one has a difficult past or reality that they must deal with forever. Discrimination towards Naruto for having the nine tails inside him and the Uchiha clan, PTSD from war and a loss of comrades, and so on. Real life aspects that are expressed onto this story.

On a personal level, this show has brought much inspiration, strength and reconciliation that has truly changed my teenage years as a whole. 

Overall this show is recommended to everyone, especially for those who are into history, philosophy, literature, mythology , cool fights scenes or simply someone who yearns for the light in times of darkness. 

Thank you Kishimoto and all the animators who participated in this masterpiece of art.

I should mention that I binge-watched this show and skipped about 95% of the fillers. I will try to keep this review spoiler free. Naruto Shippuden takes place about 2.5 years after the events which transpired in the original Naruto series. Sasuke Uchiha deserted the Hidden Leaf Village and joined up with the sinister Orochimaru to gain more power in his quest to kill his brother and avenge his family. Naruto Uzumaki decided to train with Jiraiya in order to improve his skill so he could get Sasuke back to his side. Meanwhile the threat of the organization called Akatsuki drives ever closer, who areout to capture Naruto.

The story is rarely the strong point of a shonen anime. It often comes down to a villain who is drunk on power and who wants to take control of the world. In that regard Naruto Shippuden is not that much different. At the start it’s simple, but effective. Without spoiling too much I found that the story did get a bit too convoluted at the end, but I imagine it can be difficult to try and wrap it all up. 

I will say however that almost each villain has his own unique reason for why they want to achieve world domination. In some cases, I found myself even sympathizing with the villains. The line between good and bad is blurry and often there are flashbacks which explain why a villain has had a change of heart and why he or she has those different ideologies. There are a lot of interesting and tragic themes such as pain, isolation and destiny. These different motivations bring more depth to the villains. 

This is why I found the characters to be the best part of the show. There is the typical shonen protagonist Naruto Uzumaki. He is a total goofball, yet very dependable at the same time. He works and trains the hardest and he has the ability to connect with other people. He’s a good main character and I found myself cheering for him throughout the whole show. Sasuke Uchiha at the other hand is the complete opposite of Naruto. He is “cool”, very talented, all the girls swoon over him, but he struggles with himself and mainly with his past. Even throughout the original Naruto show I found Sasuke to be a very polarizing character. At points I disliked him and at other points I sort of liked him. This trend continued for me in Naruto Shippuden. 

Then there are a lot of other characters, who all have their own powers and weaknesses. We of course have all the Hidden Leaf Ninjas. We get introduced to ninjas from other villages. Some characters from the past get more fleshed out. Finally, we have the villains. I already made mention of the them up above. Pain and Itachi are some of my favorite characters in any anime ever. So, all in all that leaves us with more than 50 important characters. All of them are unique and you’ll find yourself picking favorites for some of these characters. Some of them focus on long distance, while others are hand to hand combat specialists. If you watched the original Naruto you will know there is a big difference between a Shikamaru or a Rock Lee fight. 

The main problem with having so many characters however is that not every character gets developed or his/her time to shine. In the original Naruto show we saw minor characters having proper 1 on 1 fights during the Chunin Exams and during the Sasuke Recovery arcs. They got multiple episodes and often you saw flashbacks of their pasts. This way you got interested in some of those characters and you had your favorites. Because so many new characters get introduced during Shippuden – and since we do not have THAT many villains – some of these ninjas do not get any fights during the whole of Shippuden. This is a shame since I was invested in some of them and subsequently didn’t get to see if they learned new techniques or improved. Their characters in effect didn’t develop much / at all. 

In addition, there is also a bit too much powering up going on to my liking. The fighting, the techniques and the damage inflicted all get turned up a few scales. Some characters even get buffed/evolve multiple times during one fight, which makes them literally (demi) gods. Other characters meanwhile stay behind. I believe this is called power creep?
Another strong point of this show is the setting, the world of Naruto. How someone can come up with ideas and concepts like ninja villages, ninjutsu, genjutsu, kages, tailed beasts and how all that stuff is connected, is beyond me. It’s genius and it’s all carefully laid out and explained in this show. 

Just like in the original Naruto show, the soundtrack is amazing. There are some tracks which will pump you up for another great fight, and there are tracks which will hit you right in the feels. There are 20 different openings and 40 different endings. I’m sure you will find something you like and dislike. Personally, I liked the opening track called Silhouette by KANA-BOON the most. 
The animation is good. It can be a bit inconsistent and there is an obvious change of pace when high action episodes occur. I like the style of animation which gets used during those high actions episodes. It is more fluid, but I could understand if people didn’t like it. The fights and more specifically the hand to hand combat scenes are often amazing; even mesmerizing. I don’t like it though when the animation in openings already spoil upcoming events or matchups. This happened a couple of times.   

I feel like I also should mention something about the fillers. I binge-watched Naruto Shippuden and I skipped 95% of the fillers. I recommend you to do the same. Naruto Shippuden is a masterful continuation of Naruto's story, and as a series it even manages to improve upon its' predecessor - an anime which already needed little improving, in my opinion. Still, it has its' own drawbacks which will be off putting for some viewers, which I'll go over. The story provides more of the action adventure found in Naruto, while the plot really matures appropriate to the characters' ageing up. The mysterious Akatsuki organisation establish a threat right from the start, while maintaining suspense through many episodes as each character is revealed slowly, one at a time. These villains provide situations that feel trulyperilous for our heroes, and the show packs in a solid handful of emotional gut-punches throughout.
The arcs are varied enough to hold the viewer's interest across a long series, and bring focus to characters other than Naruto; as well as battling Akatsuki members, there are arcs focused on Naruto's training, on Sasuke's activities, or on revealing important mysteries and backstories.
Now, there are still weak points to the story. There are some overpowered techniques conveniently used, such as Izanagi, Rinne Rebirth, or the 100 Healings. Several times characters are saved from certain death by such powers. While this might be an annoyance for viewers at times, ultimately I think Naruto has enough tragedy in its premise and across Shippuden's story, without becoming bleak by piling up too many corpses of beloved characters.
Towards the end the story does teeter on the edge of the trap of 'too many villain reveals': "I'm the villain- no I'M the real villain- no, fools, it was me all along!". This isn't Shippuden's strongest hour, but it does serve to add a cool sense of destiny and fated conflict for our heroes, so if you enjoy that kind of element in stories, you won't be displeased. And - ultimately - the real final conflict is the one you knew was coming since the very beginning of Naruto, and when it comes at long last, it won't disappoint. To me, it delivers an emotionally charged and satisfying payoff to a series which I have followed for many years, and it's an arc I am happy to rewatch regularly.
Overall, there are no unanswered questions left at the end, no frustrating ambiguity, and I think it is well worth spending 500 episodes to reach such a satisfying conclusion.

The characters have always been Naruto's strongest asset, and that's no different in Shippuden. Our protagonists have spent time becoming stronger, they're more emotionally mature and (sometimes) wiser. My favourite example of this development across the time skip is Sakura, who really comes into her own in Shippuden. There is still plenty of room for growth for them across the series, and we get to see many of the large cast shine on their own. The histories of some fan favourite characters are slowly revealed, to great effect, any many new characters are added to the cast.
By far and away the greatest of these new additions is that most beloved villain organisation in anime: the Akatsuki! And they're beloved for good reason. They are equal parts intimidating and badass; at times even goofy. They range from sympathetic anti-heroes, to assholes who are having so much fun being assholes that you can't help but love them a little bit. Each member is given adequate screen time to showcase their unique abilities and personalities, but even so, they're so enjoyable to spend time with that it's almost bittersweet to see them defeated; I just can't get enough of watching them.
Of course, within any show, not every character can be perfect, and for me in Shippuden, Karin really takes the crown as the worst character in the entire Naruto-verse. Constantly annoying and adds nothing to the plot. Fortunately she is only a minor character, so we're not overrun with screen time for her. Conversely, the character of Killer B, who I admit I find tiresome at times in the manga, I actually find less annoying and more tolerable in the anime.
The last thing I'll mention in terms of character is the slight pitfall which I think Shippuden falls into during it's latter half; that is a still expanding cast of less important characters. While they retain unique and memorable character design, the addition of a new set of characters from the nations neighbouring the Land of Fire ultimately doesn't add all that much to the story. I think this is because there isn't enough time to develop them much at the late stage of the anime, and they end up relying largely on gimmicks rather than fleshed out personalities (examples are the Fifth Mizukage and Omoi). This just means that if these characters are in peril, it's hard to care too much about it.

The music in this series is absolutely outstanding. There is a new composer, Yasuhara Takanashi, who continues many elements and themes as to feel like a seamless transition between series, while introducing many beautiful pieces of his own, and appropriately badass character themes for many new villains. Some of the most standout tracks of the OST are Senya (or Many Nights), Girei, and Hyouhaku (or Wandering). It's an OST that I have continued to listen to frequently for more than 10 years.
Of the many opening songs, a couple are average; the rest range from good to brilliant. The best ones do their job of pumping you up for the action, and provide an emotional kick for viewers invested in the characters. The best examples of this are Blue Bird, Sign, Diver, and Silhouette. Special mention also goes to Hero's Come Back!!, which was perfectly chosen as the first opening of Shippuden. It you come to this anime after Naruto and aren't pumped already, then this opening does that job for you - the song coupled with animation that includes a really badass shot of the mysterious Akatsuki organisation is enough to get anyone excited.
To note; I watch the English dub, and I enjoy it immensely. I have still watched plenty of episodes in Japanese, as for most of the time I watched it the English dubbed episodes were a little behind the Japanese release; I don't think there's any notable shift in tone or quality between the two, so whichever one you prefer I think will be equally enjoyable. A notable mention goes to Vic Mignogna and Michael Yurchack who both voice versions of a character who is introduced later in the series, and stood out to me as unique and memorable voices for an important character.

There's little to say about the art other than: it's just good. It's pleasant to look at, and the fight scenes are visually exciting. The lines look cleaner than it's predecessor. The palette retains a lot of it's vibrancy, though it becomes desaturated through certain arcs appropriate to the tone of the story, as our heroes face more serious threats and losses.

The main drawback of Shippuden is much the same as Naruto's: an excessive amount of filler. And unlike it's predecessor the filler arcs are interspersed throughout the main story, so if you are intent on avoiding them, it takes a little more effort to do so (i.e. looking up filler lists online). However, I would say that some of the filler is quite enjoyable; the different tailed-beast arcs, Kakashi's Anbu arc, and Itachi's Shinden arc spring to mind. Also, a lot of the filler in later episodes tries to delve into some of the supporting characters, rather than being just meaningless monster-of-the-week fodder. Additionally, some later filler arcs are actually based on light novels that accompany the manga, rather than being anime-only.
Ultimately, I think the filler isn't as big an issue for new viewers as it was for fans watching along as episodes were released (it could certainly make you impatient when waiting for the story to advance, back in the day); but any new viewer can use their discretion to decide whether to watch or skip ahead.

Overall, Naruto and Shippuden have retained their position as my favourite anime of all time since I first started watching, more than a decade ago. I love being immersed in the world and I find the central themes and conflicts to be heartening, and emotionally satisfying. There are several arcs that I enjoy rewatching regularly on their own, and at any given point I'm itching to rewatch the whole series again, filler and all.

For fans of Naruto I think it's highly worth seeing how the story develops and concludes in Shippuden. For viewers who are reluctant to watch Naruto (maybe it seems a little young) and want to jump in at Shippuden, I think it's possible. The backstories of the characters are revisited enough that it's probably not too hard to understand or follow, though I do think you'd be missing out on some critical character bonding from the first part.

This review is for all of the Naruto series. "a 7/10 show with 12/10 moments." This quote, along with the addition of some 10/10 characters, sums up my experience with the Naruto series pretty well. I am in no way saying that Naruto Shippuuden along with it's prequel are flawless pieces of media, in fact far from it, but I cannot ignore the lasting impact this show managed to place on me. I believe it's important to take this show for what it is rather than allow ourselves to be blinded by nostalgia, so to quickly bring up some of the problems within the series I'llstart with the frankly terrible writing of majority of the female characters. It is no secret that the girls in this show have some downright pitiful writing compared to the male ones, and there really isn't any way to excuse that. Throughout the majority of the show the girl characters seem to be used as plot devices to help forward the development of the primarily male cast, and seeing as Naruto is a battle shounen, this unfortunately comes as little surprise to me. Aside from this obvious fault, the other main problem that I'm sure everyone has heard much about is the sheer amount of filler. It is an undeniable fact that if your show is 700+ episodes long with over 40% of those being filler, there's a problem. This being said however, I understand why this was done, and don't see a problem if you choose to skip the filler episodes as Naruto is already a long series as is. Personally however, as long as I like the characters, I can find enjoyment in some filler arcs, that is if they are not shoved in the middle of an important story arc.

There are other flaws such as the poor writing of the over 200 episode long war arc and the lack luster finale of this serious commitment of a show, but setting aside the bad lets touch on what makes this series so good. 

My love for the Naruto series stems from the pure attachment you get to it's characters, I mean how can you not after spending 720 episodes watching them grow and achieve their goals, as well as suffer from loss and hardships. It may sound cheesy, but after basically growing up with these characters for years of my childhood, they hold a special place in my heart, and therefore the impact of character death or growth hits that much harder. 

Something I really commend the Naruto series for is the writing of the "villains." They have you questioning what is truly good and evil, with most all the villains having a clear and sometimes rather convincing motive for why they do what they do, which is something I don't see too often in shows. Often times in media villains are just chocked up to the baseless cliche of "taking over the world" or just being downright comically evil, but I don't see that happening in Naruto. It is really hard to hate most of this shows antagonists, as you find yourself questioning whether these "bad guys" are really all that bad. In a classic battle of ideologies mixed with some beautifully choreographed fight scenes, the clash between the expansive cast of equally lovable characters is something you can't look away from.

Aside from the villains, the rivalry explored between our main characters, Naruto and Sasuke, is what I believe to be one of the most enthralling dynamics in all of shounen. Watching the unbroken dance of emotions surrounding these two as they combat each other in passionate battles of skill and wit, as well as the internal mental conflict that they each face, is one of the most emotionally investing stories that I've had the joy of experiencing. Between the constant battle of love and hatred they feel for one another and the shattered bonds they share with their own home and family, the war going on within these two boys' minds and hearts is sincerely something to behold. It truly is a wonderful journey of growth and acceptance that while full of pain and heartbreak along the way, ultimately reaches a a conclusion that is wholeheartedly worth it. I find myself going back to watch the finale of their concluding fight more than I'd like to admit, but it's just that good. This iconic duo is one that is sure to be remembered for years to come. 

TLDR; Naruto has the power to make you fall head over heels for it's characters and world, you'll find yourself laughing and crying along side them, and before you know it the once daunting series may start to not feel as long. By the end I was yearning for more, wishing to see my favorite shinobi go on more adventures together, strengthening their bonds, experiencing joys and sorrows, and most of all continuing to make the Naruto series what it is; an experience worth remembering. 

I can safely say that while Naruto has undoubtedly gone down in history as one of the most iconic anime series out there, the lessons and emotions that came along with it will be forever etched in our hearts as well.

Naruto is my favorite anime of all time. I've been following it since 2010 and since then, I've watched many animes. Still, nothing compares to it. Attack on Titan may come as second, but it's no way near it. The theme is just too brilliant. It's something that never ever came into my mind. I really like the world of ninjas depicted in this show. I like the idea of Jutsu and Chakra. I love the fights. I love the backstories of each character. The characters' development is incredibly consistent. The show will fill you with many emotions: inspiring, charming, funny, sad, etc. The arcs and fightswill blow your mind: it's strategic, a trait that many others lack; it's wholesome, not just punching around like a sh*t or throwing random powers like Dragon Ball and One Piece. I have too many favorite fights and arcs that make it impossible to list here, but the best one is certainly The Pain Invasion. 

That being said, sadly this amazing show has to suffer from many of what I call "anime's fallacies". They are defects that lower the anime's potential. These didn't happen very often, tho, gladly. But, I'm a very logical person, and I love to have a show to be logical if it's meant to be.

- The main characters shall not be dead because we'll lose many fans / we cannot make up their subsequent story.
- Forget about side characters, just let them be punching bags.
- Mouthful during fights. The characters bother explaining his plot after defeating his opponent (they did this so that the viewer can also understand, but it's nonsense. It should be explained with flashback).
- Show the greatness of the villain by nerfing (making weak) the good characters.
- The level of power has to increase dramatically over time (you know, in the Naruto series, kunai and shuriken were still a weapon to kill enemies. In Shippuden, they were just an adornment).

The first fallacy makes many illogical events happen. (spoiler alert! skip this paragraph if you haven't watched yet). Because of the author's insistence on keeping the main characters alive, Gaara and Kakashi had to be revived by some weird Jutsu. Choji and Ino didn't die after being suffocated by Kakuzu. Sasuke didn't die after being stabbed by Madara on his heart. All five kages didn't die after being knocked down by Madara. C'mon, have the courage to kill them. Did Death Note lose his fanbase after killing L, its favorite character? Did AOT lose after killing Sasha and Captain Erwin?

The last fallacy is what I dislike most. It went from Zabuza's level -> Pain's level -> Madara's level -> Kaguya's level. In the last arc, they were just fighting against aliens and throwing a bunch of unknown jutsus, making the show like Dragon Ball which really undermined strategy. I have no idea why Kishi had this in mind. I hope it stopped at Madara's level where the fights were still consumable.

All in all, I don't find any anime without defects. If Kishi had the second chance to remake this show, I think it'll become unequivocally the greatest anime ever.

This anime is by far my favorite, and I don't think there'll be anything that will surpass it. Though, I will admit it isn't overall perfect, but what anime is. All that matters that in my eyes I believe it to be the best and that's my opinion. Story- 9/10 The story in Shippuden, while not extremely complex like some anime, it still contains underlying tones and messages in its arcs that make you think. It starts off immediately into an entertaining arc that once it starts the series never looks back. There wasn't an arc that I can say I didn't enjoy (excluding filler), some areeven my favorite arcs in all of anime, and while they mainly dealt with Naruto and Sasuke, the arcs also gave other characters development and growth that you don't see in a lot of series. The results of each arc are felt and have lasting effects on the characters and me as a viewer. Some arcs made me cry, some cheer, and some even caused me to reflect on life. Character deaths are meaningful and aren't something that are just brushed past, they are talked about and impact the series the rest of the show. The world is expanded upon and so is the lore that makes a somewhat smaller world larger and enhances it in the process. 

Art- 8.5/10

The animation in this show is its weakest point, but I wouldn't call it a negative. There are moments where you can see the flaws in certain scenes, where characters are making weird faces. Other than that the animation is good and the fight scenes are very well done with the visuals looking extremely good and the characters animated well. The fight scenes especially are amazing, with the attacks looking great, and the choreography of the fights can be among the best.

Sound- 10/10

The ost for Shippuden is among the best with emotional scenes being enhances by the background music, the fights feeling more intense because of it, and the comedic scenes better. So, the soundtrack does what it's supposed to do, enhances the overall anime. It is also, so good that I listen to a lot of them in my free time outside of watching the anime.

Characters- 10/10

Now we are on the strongest point of Shippuden, the cast of characters. Naruto and Sasuke are my favorite characters in anime, along with a couple of the supporting characters being in my top 20. Naruto and Sasuke are very well layered characters that change with what they experience around them, making them feel very human. Their bond is also something to love because they are the best pair of characters in anime, with how they interact with each other. Then, there's the supporting cast like; Kakashi, Shikamaru, Might Guy, Jiraiya, etc. Most get developed, some more than others, but it helps make you care more about these characters and what they go through in the story. Lastly there's the villains, which are also extremely strong characters, who have their own backstories and reasons for what they do. It makes you understand them, sympathize with them, and even agree with some of the points that they make. So, overall the characters are one of the major reasons that I enjoyed Shippuden. 

Enjoyment- 10/10

If you couldn't tell based off of what I wrote before this, I enjoy Shippuden to the fullest degree. Enough that I re-watched it twice and still got the same enjoyment out of it that I had the first time I watched it. 

Overall- 10/10 

So, overall I think that this is the best anime out there. Obviously this is my opinion and everyone has a right to their own. However, I request that you give it a chance if you haven't already, and I hope you get the same enjoyment out of it as I did.

Naruto: Shippuden for me, is considered to be an era-defining show; It was something that was culturally influential for the time it was established and arguably STILL is to this day, and has helped shape what anime is generally today. Its by no means a perfect show, and that's what the detail of this review is for. But for what it is, it's something I do recommend people to watch and find themselves to invest their time in when they could. Animation (8/10) - This was a show that ran from 2007 - 2017; Standing the test of time generally, it's animation style is starting tobecome definitive for its time. It doesn't hurt the viewing experience that much imo, but I do have to say: In comparison to its continuation, Naruto (2002), this one have a noticeably better quality. The movements of the characters are more fluid, and has a more expressive tones onto it. 

I guess the only criticism I have is Studio Pierrot Co. (its producers), must've started slacking or doing budget cuts at the later parts of its run after The Great War arc concluded because its definition plummeted at around 480-500 episodes deep with some characters lacking details and shading as they used to. But for the majority of its run, I think they did a good job.

Storyline (9/10) - Compared to Naruto (2002), this one has a much RICHER storyline. It still bottomlines on the occurrence of The Great War, but all the major arcs that leads slowly onto that progression is seriously action-packed and filled with sensational expositions. A lot of its side characters, especially the antagonists are also well-written in terms of their backstories, purposes and so, that you can't help but appreciate both the spectrum of good and evil as the conflicts unfolds. Also has a lot of blowing and major deaths so, keep your heads up for that.

I guess one of the major flaw that I have that kept it from being a 10: Is the excruciating filler episodes and arcs they have. And sometimes they even come along in the MIDDLE of the main arc! As a breather I suppose or to extend their runtime? Idk but it's definitely annoying. Just like Naruto (2002), sometimes it would only be a couple of episodes which can be bearable but there are instances where it could span up to 10-12 eps or something. So it's like a Russian Roulette. And oftentimes those fillers don't even have any direct affect to the main story, so its basically just a waste of time. Definitely the drawback to its perfection.

Music (9/10) - Having ten years of total time to simmer on the kitchen, it definitely had a lot of time to cook a lot of bangers and a versatile soundtrack library. It still has its trademark of Traditional Japanese-like thematic mostly on its background music that implements a rich flavor of woodwind, strings and percussion harmonies.

But in terms of OSTs, it invested a lot on Japanese Rock which they did very well because a lot of the famous songs associated with the show came from this type of genre. Most notably Blue Bird, Silhouette, Sign and more, typically relying on fast-paced guitar riffs, crashing drums and snares, raw and energetic vocals into a singularity of a melody; The type of thing that would make your head bang and get drawn onto the tunes. Watching 40 episodes a day, it was the drug that anesthetized my pain and entertained my loneliness. Sometimes I felt like Rock Lee, a boy who due to a genetic disease is unable to be a normal ninja, but even so through absolute effort and dedication to training, he keeps his dream active through a will towin. Or like Neji, who as a member of the warrior part of the Hyuuga clan is destined to serve the noblest part. Becoming someone indifferent to fate, until a punch to the chin changes his perspective.

 Kishimoto - author of the work - through his characters assumes the positions of father, grandfather, brother and or teacher. Naruto is a great deep motivational speech about how hard life is, and people need to have the strength to overcome it, which I needed at that time.
In Naruto and Naruto Shippuden, the ninja world is a constant war between humans and their traumatic lives. Orchestrated by battles of jutsu, kunais, shurikens, swordsmen, clashes of giant animals, colossal demons inhabiting the bodies of young people and a lot of flashback, while the soundtrack makes a point of tearing every tear from your eyelid or stretching every inch of your lip through smiles in moments of happiness.
The exaggeration in praising the relationship between Naruto and Sasuke with constant reruns and memories, good characters becoming extras, the inconstant animation and the exaggerated fillers weaken the brightness of their journey.
But it would be impossible, not to be grateful for the story and appreciate its great deeds and characters that welcomed me when I needed it most.
