Summary; It balances between all the aspects that make a good show (animation, osts, story, themes, characters etc.) perfectly and has very little flaws. Decent story, likeable characters, adventure in a beautiful atmospheric world, interesting fantasy elements/concepts, philosophical themes, mysteries/conspiracies/plot twists, cool action scenes and epic moments, its has everything. As a result this anime has a very broad appeal. The good points: It does almost everything right (story, characters, themes etc.) Really shines out in terms of: Consistency of quality Crazy pay offs for build-ups or shocking scenes that come out of nowhere (epic moments) Diverse atmospheric steampunk world Exploring fantasy elements through a scientific or research based manner Plot-twist/mysteryreveals/conspiracies
Melodious osts perfect for various types of scenes
A long adrenaline fueled final arc involving a massive showdown between the good guys and the bad guys, which converges (and terminates) numerous character arcs as well.

The bad points: 
A few of the fantasy elements feel random or don't make much sense.
One fantasy element which is a rule of this show's magic system (alchemy) is inconsistent with a military law and something that happens in the beginning of the show.
The pilot and a few episodes at the beginning aren't as good as the rest of the show and are somewhat rushed compared to the source material.
It gets slightly slow or loses momentum at one point in the middle of the series.
The main villain is slightly underwhelming.



Story: The story is fine.
An atmospheric steampunk fantasy involving lots of lively  and likeable characters with different but understandable motivations, all of which are in some way or the other related to a nation's government with many dark secrets.
The story also involves a little bit of lore like a little bit of mythology, a war that happened in recent history, an abrupt fall of a civilization etc. All this adds more depth to the story.

The use of interesting concepts that require detailed explanation which drive the story (like those based on country relations, economy, fantasy, sci-fi elements etc.), themes of the story depicted in a natural manner, multiple subplots involving fleshed out characters with conflicting and understandable motivations interwoven with each other, interesting situations created naturally involving high tension etc. makes a story interesting and complex. FMAB handles these things pretty good.

Themes: After giving much thought, I can say that the themes are handled perfectly. All the themes it raises like 'flying too close to the sun', 'the value of a human soul' or 'to gain something, something of equal value must be sacrificed' are integrated very naturally in the story and are depicted through various events. The arrogant desires of human to bend the laws of nature for their gain irrespective of how much sacrifice it requires is what starts and further drives the story. The bitter consequences of it (flying too close to the sun) and the sacrifice for the sake of something truly invaluable for us as humans is how it ends. I can't elaborate on it without spoiling so I'll leave it at that but just from reading this much one can tell, how thematically consistent and well planned the story is. Nothing is forced. Furthermore all the character have a certain central idea or theme associated with them as explained in characters section.


Characters: Characters are fine.
The characters are sufficiently fleshed out i.e. they show different emotions that you would expect them to in a given situation so they don't come across as one dimensional. Their relationship/behavior with each other also varies depending upon the pair. No character sticks too unrealistically closely to a single trait. All characters have a unique personality with respect to each other.

Their personality is complimented by their respective character design i.e. most characters look how you would expect them to based on their personality.

The characters have understandable motivations and their actions are consistent with those motivations.

No character is obnoxious and many of them from the good side can even be likeable including the MC duo.

Many character have certain main ideas associated with them like duty vs humanity, guilt, vengeance, handling of power of evil origin etc. The ideas or traits to be more precise associated with the secondary villains are the seven sins they are named after but they aren't one dimensional by any means. The termination of their arcs with respect to the idea they represent is done perfectly and involve a great sense of irony for almost all of them except lust. These characters explore these ideas throughout their story.

All character arcs converge in an epic finale very smoothly. No character is ignored. Even the relatively minor characters aren't ignored. MC grows in maturity (and height) gradually that you wouldn't even notice. Everyone gets some lesson related to the ideas associated with them or what you call development till the end.

The main villain however while not bad by any means may feel somewhat underwhelming when compared to other villains which is to say that he doesn't strike as particularly interesting or menacing for all the hype created. The theme associated with him however is explored perfectly. 



Fantasy: The fantasy elements are pretty sensible and interrelated by anime standard

The fantasy elements mainly consists of alchemy and a small mythology. 
Alchemy is of 2 types: normal and soul alchemy
Normal alchemy can be used to change shape and volume of substances by making a transmutation circle. When used in fights it can be pretty creative.
Soul alchemy is slightly more complex. It is a pretty interesting concept that has been used multiple times in the show.

There are many research related to alchemy involving alchemy to produce interesting results like secret to immortality, philosohper's stone, human transmutation, giagantic transmutation circle, flame alchemy, alkahistory, scar's (one of the character) alchemy, body armor, chimeras etc. These research related things are pretty sensible and add more intrigue to the show. Its one of the best aspects of the show.

The fantasy elements have a certain look to them which distinguish them from other series. Red lightning, the way matter disintegrates, magical eyes that we see many times in the show, tangible shadows etc. look very unique, iconic that just by looking at them you can tell that they are from fmab. I really like it when a series has a unique set of fantasy elements similar to how light sabers from star wars look iconic.

However a law of alchemy says that the nature of substances can't be changed using alchemy. However the MC in one episode converted coal to gold. Plus there's a military law that prohibits such activities. If it was possible to change nature of matter, the MCs could've found easier alternatives to certain situations. The author made a mistake here.
Another minor thing i find weird is that flame alchemy can't be used when its source that is spark creating gloves with transmutation circle drawn on them is wet. Sparks can be created even in rain so it doesn't make much sense.

Coming to the mythology part. It isn't very elaborated. The main villain's origins isn't explained but thats one of the things that he himself was looking for so its ok.

The thing that i find somewhat weird is that using soul alchemy the villain splits his personality into 7 sins of Christianity and imbues them in a human body's soul to take control over that body, and also imbues it with philosopher stone (a fantasy object of power in the show) to give them random powers and regenerative abilities after lots of experimenting. The result is called homunculus. That means in the world of fma, the soul comprises of 7 vices and virtues of Christianity. I am not fond of this concept because i feel that it might not be an entirely comprehensive classification with mutually exclusive classes/groups and is probably outdated. For example, i think greed and gluttony (excess greed for food) aren't mutually exclusive and gluttony is a form of greed. Also we don't get to see how separation of these sins from his body changed the main villain. He clearly has lots of greed and pride even after he separated them from his body. We have to assume that he didn't remove all of it but it isn't explicitly mentioned. Infact one character once said that removing these sins from one's soul means removing one's humanity if I remember correctly. Did his pride and greed reduce after the separation? Also after seeing the origin story of the villain you can't help but wonder did he really have lust in him? One thing i do like about the separation of sins concept is that, in Christianity, in order to get closer to the God which is equivalent to truth in a symbolic way in fma and is related to the villain's motivations, one must separate themselves from the seven vices or sins which means separation of sins is a part of the process that leads the villain to his goals but he also used it to get some homunculi goons to help in the process. This is also related to one of the main themes of the show that is introduced in very early parts of the show 'flying too close to the sun' where sun can be a metaphor for God. Also I feel that the powers are too random. Their powers should be based on alchemy. However one of them has the power to control shadows and turn them into a sharp and strong weapons. It might be a cool technique but shadow is not even an object in the first place so how can he use alchemy on it? Another of the homunculus have access to another dimension which is contained in a small space but is way larger when inside. How is dimension creation related to alchemy? Two of the homunculi have access to super speed. Again how is this related to alchemy? 

Its not explained why only a few individuals have access to the doors  (fantasy object that look like doors; source of alchemy) of alchemy.


Enjoyment: Its a very enjoyable and consistent series. I'll discuss the various categories that makes it enjoyable.

Epic scenes: The epic scenes are absolutely amazing. t has lots of highly energetic epic moments (pay off for build-up or abrupt shocking scenes). These epic moments mostly involve amazing fight scenes which the audience waits for but there are many other types of epic scenes as well (like mystery reveals or involving large scale destruction in important places).


Action: The action scenes are amazing.

Its fight scenes are brief but absolutely amazing. Well choreographed, strategic and involving lots of destruction.

Alchemy makes the fight scenes somewhat diverse and unique since each alchemist has a unique power that must be used in a unique way. It doesn't involve ass-pulls or bizarre logic or strategies. Fights can involve lots of simple but clever tricks instead of some bizzare strategy that conveniently ignores physics and fantasy rules of the series with a narrator or character going on and on to justify it.

The power levels are consistent. Some characters are op (like their single touch can kill, or a snap of their fingers can burn anything or they move too fast) but thats the best part because its interesting to see how these fights will go and some massacres (one sided fights) are incredibly satisfying.



World building:
It doesn't have a detailed map.

There aren't many iconic locations that appear frequently and become of great importance. None that i remember of.

However its world is very diverse and beautiful. Its has places like a military base covered in snow, beautiful windy european countryside, tunnels with rail-tracks, beautiful old civilization etc.

The world design is detailed, atmospheric and diverse. 


Adventure: Pretty good.
Beautiful world design brimming with energy with lively characters especially the MC who are looking for answers in various places makes it a good adventure series.



Comedy:
The comedy is ok. The character interactions are comical in normal situations. Sometimes it can become philosophical. In serious moments it is suitably dark.



Mystery:
A very important aspect of the show. The MCs set out on a journey to learn about how to regain their biological body (which is replaced by metallic parts). This leads them to learn about various dark secrets related to the world they live in. We learn along with them and its really interesting to see things gradually starting to make sense. Natirally there are many plot-twists as well.
It has mystery surrounding the country the characters live in, the father of the MC duo, a war that happened recently, a major event that happened in the past that ended an entire civilization and all the research areas related to alchemy. All of these secrets are related to each other.



Music:
It has music for all kinds of situation which suit the scenes perfectly. Most of its music is orchestral and very melodious. It elevates all the scenes to greater heights and complements the beautiful artstyle. Its osts are easily among the best in a show. Also the openings and endings are very visually immersive. The voice acting is great and the dub is very good.


Animation: 
Good looking and consistent.

After having watched the first anime adaption of Fullmetal Alchemist, I couldn't help feeling a sense of disappointment at the ending. It didn't follow the manga's ending, and it showed with a poor performance. In this redone version of the manga, the anime faithfully follows its counterpart and makes for a great show. Story: 9 The story is great, but for me personally, the whole "super power" aspect of the anime almost feels a little overdone, as if I'd seen it already in many other shows. Even with this little hiccup, I still feel as though the story deserves praise for its complexities and plot twists. Art: 9 Theartwork is very solid throughout the entire anime, but doesn't really do anything innovative or exciting to deserve a 10. The character models are solid, the uniforms of the soldiers are done well, and the locations and environments are good.

Sound: 10
I'm not one to usually ever praise English audio over its Japanese counterpart, but this anime has (in my opinion) superior English voice actors. The voice actors really put emotion into their characters, especially Vic. The only problem I have is that Alphonse's voice actor from the original hit puberty and couldn't do a repeat, so they had to bring in someone new who I think didn't do quite as good a job. But suffice to say that the voice acting is superb. The sound effects are also outstanding, especially when alchemy is being performed.

Character: 9
What I really like about this anime is that the multitude of characters introduced throughout the show are handled very appropriately. Supporting characters get their back stories explained thoroughly (for the most part), and the Elric brothers get the spotlight you'd expect the main characters to get.

Enjoyment: 9
When I feel like I have to watch the next episode right away, I know that the series is great. For me, I give a 10 in enjoyment when after I finish a series, I feel profoundly blown away. I didn't get that feeling after watching FMA, but that "edge on your seat" feeling was constantly there.

Overall: 9
How many anime can you REALLY give a 10? There aren't many, because anime masterpieces should totally blow your mind after you finish them. FMA is a great anime, but not a masterpiece.

Characters: I can't stress enough how good the character development in this show is. Many shows have a strong main cast of characters and a background cast that's developed just enough for you to remember they exist. FMAB, on the other hand, has a literal army of characters that you not only remember, but actually care about. Both Edward and Alphonse are interesting to follow, Winry is the best supporting character I've ever seen (with a beautifully non forced romance between her and Ed), Mustang is arguably THE main character as a character who gets almost no screen time compared to the Elric brothers... I could keep going. If there is any reason to watch Brotherhood over the original it's the characters.

Sound: Just listen to one of the opening songs. Or endings. This show is easily a contender for the show with the best chosen music. No other shows songs has ever brought me to tears but FMAB's songs do it consistently, while the other songs hype you up for the battle between the protagonists and the Homunculi. 

Art: Look it up and judge for yourself. I think brotherhood is a beautiful show but this category is more subjective than the others.

The most important aspect of this show though, is that it isn't basic. It's core principle (Equivalent Exchange) creates a lot of thought. While watching this show you can either: zone out and watch the Elric brothers beat the **** out of everything and everybody OR actually think about the underlying themes in the show and spend some time on the show after watching it. Both ways are exciting and can suit a wide audience. 

Closing thoughts: For those who are brand new to the FMA franchise, I suggest watching Brotherhood first. Brotherhood is the prettier show, with stronger characters and better music. The original excels in it's story and most particularly it's ending. I believe that watching FMA first would spoil the experience that is Brotherhood.

Okay, I'm of two minds when it comes to this series. For starters, FMAB has an OBJECTIVELY better ending than the 2003 adaptation-I mean, there's no arguing that the ending to 2003 SUCKED, you just can't do it. And FMAB is definitely prettier to look at and has awesome music and all this stuff, and of course, IT FOLLOWS THE MANGA (yes, I'm poking fun at you, manga-purists)...but that doesn't make it perfect, by any stretch of the imagination. One of the things that I really didn't like about this anime was the pacing-at least, for the first twelve episodes or so. Maybe it's just becauseI watched the 2003 version first and literally started watching Brotherhood only a couple of days after finishing the first anime, but the first major story arc of this show felt SOOOO weird in terms of pacing. It literally felt like half of the first anime's plot condensed into a few episodes, and you might like that better, but for me, it didn't really work. The first set of episodes just felt really rushed imo, and even though the plot was fast, it didn't really pick up until later because it was just retreading the same ground that 2003 walked on. Once it gets to the introduction of Ling and a few other characters that weren't in the original anime, however, it definitely gets better and more watchable for fans of the 2003 version.

Another thing I don't like are the villains-for the most part. They're all pretty one-dimensional, cardboard cutout villains who are just evil for the sake of being evil...with two MAJOR exceptions. One thing that 2003 did better than Brotherhood (at least in my opinion) was making you CARE about the villains, to the point where you didn't want some of them to die. Brotherhood? Aside from the two exceptions I mentioned (which I won't name here in order to avoid spoilers), they didn't really accomplish that.

Now let's get onto what it did RIGHT, because remember-I still REALLY like this anime. (Though it will always be my 2ND favorite behind the original FMA) For starters, it handled the ending a lot better than the original adaptation, and, of course, it followed the manga, not that I really care. (That's NOT why I prefer Brotherhood's ending, btw. I just like that it's a lot more happy and satisfying than the ending to the original anime) It also had some really awesome fight scenes-like, no joke, they were amazing. It also had like, ZERO filler in my opinion, which cant be said for the 2003 version (which literally had an entire episode dedicated to showing us the collapse of a village caused by a deadly plague that had NOTHING to do with the actual story other than the fact that the main characters happened to be heading there to meet someone that didn't have an impact on the story anyway), so it definitely gets a thumbs up from me for that.

To sum things up, Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is more Fullmetal Alchemist, and for that I love it. It retold the story, added fun characters from the manga that didn't make it into the 2003 version due to them not existing at the time, it had a better ending, and it put a new coat of paint on one of my favorite franchises. That being said, while I REALLY LOVE this show, I think it's INCREDIBLY overrated, and I heartily recommend that you watch the 2003 version BEFORE Brotherhood. If you watch Brotherhood first, you'll most likely be put off by the original version once you try to go back and watch it, and I personally believe that in order to fully enjoy Brotherhood, you need to have at least seen a significant portion of the original.

Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is a good anime. It has interesting story and creative world but I really strugle to understand why do others consider it a masterpiece, why is rated 9.1 and why it has been top 1 anime for several years until Frieren came out. Don't get me wrong, I liked it but it doesn't stand out in any way compared to other anime. The story is good, it features some twists but it doesn't blow your mind and the emotional scenes are often predictable and didn't really hit me. There are many other shows that have better story or emotional moments. The pacingcould also be a little bit faster.

The animation is fluid and clear although the resolution is only 720p. Even then, it has aged well. The battles are fun to watch and characters' emotions are shown well but it is in no way special.

The music does its job well and I quite liked some of the tracks. But it cannot be compared to music from music-heavy shows like Made in Abyss, so clearly music can't be what makes FMAB special. I really liked the first OP song but the rest was skippable.

What about the world building? Alchemy is interesting concept but it wasn't deeply explored. Two main rules to alchemy have been laid out: you have to make a circle and you have to obey the 'law of equivalent exchange' but for the most part of the show they both have been broken one way or another. There is also some confusion about the philosopher's stone: it is supposed to be perfect with infinite amount of energy, yet when the homonculi regenerate with them, they spend them. There is also a taboo of human transmutation, when one breaks it, they "pay toll". At one point in the show one character is (not explained how) forced to break the taboo, even though they have literally done nothing they still pay the price. To me it seems the story is either not consistent with its alchemy mechanics or they are not sufficiently explained.

There are also a lot of parallels to Nazi Germany but I have no idea if there is a point behind them. Maybe it's just an inspiration but if that's the case, I feel like they were not needed at all. Surely a fictional country could commit genocide or two without the president having to be called Führer.

So in the end, I haven't found Fullmetal Alchemist's secret. To me nothing stands out as outstandingly original, unique or perfect. It's a good show so go ahead and watch it. Just lower your expectations a bit.

When it comes to this title, it needs little, if any, introduction. Everybody knows Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood. It is famous for the indelible impact it had on otaku culture, and the enduring profile it has in the community even today. Many people grew up with this anime, and so did I, but I didn't give it a proper watchthrough until years later. Indeed, Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is my 100th anime, so even while I am able to recognize its flaws, it still holds a special place in my life, and I believe it has broadly earned its fame and acclaim.Beginning with the story, this anime boasts a unique and fascinating world with a hard magic system in which to set its tale, serving as a strong cornerstone upon which the rest of the story is built. It then adds a compelling and existential conspiracy over the top of a strongly executed shonen journey, and manages to keep the story engaging from start to finish. This anime knows exactly when to hit all of its story beats, and many of the big reveals are still talked about even today, as they were both  memorable in general and formative to many early anime fans in particular. In short, the story is engaging, creative, and satisfying. You can really sink your teeth into it, all while it somehow remains accessible to those new to anime, without losing even a bit of its character. It is for this reason that the story is this anime's strongest aspect. It strikes a genuinely impressive balance between quality and accessibility, thus leaving a mark on anime history that is going to be visible forever. A true achievement, even if some of its morals and messages can be somewhat predictable, some arcs have bad pacing, and the final episode after the epilogue feels a little rushed, panicking to tie up any loose ends. 

     Now, while the story is the capstone of this show, it is brought to life by an extremely compelling art style. It manages to capture this signature 'look' throughout, which helps this anime to stand out, and grab the eye of any viewer which happens upon a screenshot or a scene on its own. It is colorful, creative, and kinetic from start to finish, and gives a potent visual identity that helps to cement this anime's legacy. It gets everything right, even crowds of background characters, making the world feel huge and three-dimensional. Its fight choreography, too, is cool and characteristic. In this way, it manages to forge technical and complex scenes of combat, balancing martial expression with alchemy, which has a physicality and vital energy all its own. I'd say its visual shot composition speaks to a kind of operatic streak throughout, a decision which is utterly unique. Indeed, I'd say it is thanks to the level of artistic vision on display here that Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood has one of the most iconic fight scenes in all of anime. I have a particular fiery instance in mind, but the fact that those of you who have watched the show before are imagining your own favorite fight scene, goes to show how excellent the art for this show is, down to the last detail. It's not even so much the quality, per se, but rather how this show allocates its resources so as to forge such extremely memorable moments.

     Then, as the art brings the story to life, the sound brings the art to life. I must begin with the fact that Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is perhaps one of the best dubs in anime history, and as such it joins the select group of titles for which I firmly recommend the dub. The sounds of life are also extremely impressive, capturing everything from shoes on cobblestone and distant traffic, all the way to the gory snapping of tendons and the magical hum of alchemy. The music also powerfully comes to bat, every episode bookended by a series of amazing OPs and EDs, not a single one of which I skipped, and a soaring classical score throughout, a true masterwork of the composer Akira Senju. 

     Finally, the characters are extremely strong for a popular shonen, even if the field gets a bit cramped at times, due to a variety of reasons. Perhaps it is because the show manages to imbue even the most minor characters with emotional weight and thematic depth, or perhaps it is because their dialogue is so human and believable, or perhaps even that their designs are so distinct and expressive. It is nearly impossible to choose favorites from among such a vibrant cast. From such compelling supporting characters like Maes Hughes, Barry the Chopper, Dr. Knox, Envy, and Greed, all the way up to the Elric brothers, Van Hohenhiem, Roy Mustang, King Bradley, and Father, the bottom line is that they are all great, and every last one of them is executed so well that the entirety of the cast and the sum total of all their individual stories will stay with the viewer for a long time. Even Sheska, that overlooked and overworked MVP. Overall, Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is one of the great works of anime, not because of any masterpiece-level production quality, but because of how it uses what it's been given, and plays to the strengths of its story. So, no matter who you are or where you are in your journey with the medium- be it your 1st or 100th title- I can absolutely recommend it.

Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood (Bones) Part 1: (Episodes 1-13) Sometimes I wish this show went full edge-lord and took the dark topics that it has and rolled with them while omitting the goofy cringe anime humor. (See that section below) But at the same time, I love the Elric brother's relationship with each other and their backstory. And even though Lieutenant Colonel Hughes was annoying at times, I did like his character, and like that his death is sparking a darker tone in the story, and am curious to see how the brothers react to it. The show has a lot of potential. I am enjoying it,but I feel like it will grow in quality in its upcoming seasons. 6/10

Part 2: (Episodes 14-26) As I suspected, the show really gets kicked into gear upon the death of Hughes which thrusts us into a political thriller with Homunculi entities as enemies which exhibit traits of the Seven Deadly Sins. Early on the show did a good job of making me mistrust Colonel Mustang before letting us know how brilliant he's going to be. He's wildly outmatched against an enemy that has powers that we can't even fathom, but so long as he's still breathing, he's a guy that you can't count out. He reminds me of Captain Levi from Attack on Titan and he's a badass that is easy to root for. As for the Elric brothers, Ed still is prone to his childish outbursts, but the duo go through some heavy character growth when they revisited their old teacher and inevitably get lumped into Mustang's plot to stop the Homunculi. I suspected that the show was going to get better, but I never anticipated it getting better this fast and staying consistent. The themes of the show get darker each episode with the philosophical question of what makes us human and what the value of a soul is being asked in a variety of ways. Unlike season 1, this season ends at an appropriate time leaving a lot of questions left unanswered and a few encounters awaiting the brothers with their father. God damn that "Let It All Out" song hit me in the feelz right there at the end. 9/10

Part 3: (Episodes 27-39) The show continues to be strong as it builds upon the fantastic season 2. We get the backstory on the Ishvalon War, our heroes are halted in their plans of overthrowing the Fuhrer, and the Homunculi's plans of creating a new Philosopher's Stone seem to be progressing while Colonel Mustang tries to fight from the shadows with his allies purposefully scattered by the Fuhrer. Scar and May Chang try to find out the purpose of his brother's research in the hopes of getting vengeance on those that caused the Ishvalon genocide while Ed and Al continue looking into how to get their bodies back with their new lead being the alchemy of the Ishvalons somehow being unaffected by the Homunculi's temporary blockage. There's a lot of intrigue in this season and it continues to build up to bigger and better things... 9/10

Part 4: (Episodes 40-52) Kimblee is an awesome antagonist. I love how he is limited in what he can do to the Elrics because of working for the Homunculi but he still suspects them every step of the way and even was even willing to kill Ed to get what he wanted. The Dwarf in the Flask episode which gave the backstory on Johenheim will go down as one of the best episodes in the series. Excellent backstory! I was so glad to see Envy finally taken down. Scar and Dr. Marcoh working together to destroy his Philosopher's Stone was awesome and with all of the atrocities that Envy has done, it was about time that humanity got a little revenge.

I don't get why the Dwarf in the Flask keeps making Greeds since he actively works against him and he knows it, but I am glad that he does because he is a lot of fun to watch. Plus with Ling Yao's body being the construct for the Philosopher's Stone, having Yao fight from the inside adds a whole new dynamic to the homunculi which already makes that even more interesting. Then having him team up with Ed and get in a showdown with Pride the most terrifying of the Homunculi? Yeah, that was all awesome. Then as always, Colonel Mustang keeps getting himself backed into a corner but just when you think he's down for the count, he flips the script with an elaborate scheme and finds a way to come out on top. They have yet to interact, but I would love to see Mustang duke it out with Kimblee. It all builds up to a final stand to prevent the day of reckoning... 9/10

Part 5: (Episodes 53-64 ) The beginning episodes were frustrating. On the one hand, it has some super powerful moments and the story remains fascinating. And everything about the eclipse and the Father's quest to become the perfect being was awesome. But it becomes way too Shonen for its own good and it drives me nuts. And for the life of me, I can not understand why Mustang does not use his flames more. He could have mowed down the mannequin horde, burned the super-soldiers to a crisp along with the scientist, and hell, he had a shot at Bradley when he was talking. But he chose to fight hand-to-hand until it was too late in all of those scenarios. It was so annoying. But boy was that Envy scene super satisfying! I was so pissed when Edward stopped him.

The season picks up for the better once all five sacrifices were brought to the Homunculus Father and he initiated the summoning circle and tried to become a God. While it was peak Shonen levels of fighting, it was actually really interesting because of the cosmic horror aspects and because the tone went from goofy to super serious with a couple character deaths including Greed, my favorite Homunculus. And above all, the show was an epic journey and it was nice to be rewarded by having a satisfying ending. So overall, I think this season has some amazing highs and it was still entertaining, but the writing wasn't as great as the last three seasons.
8/10


Plot: It's the 20th century and alchemy, the study of deconstructing and reconstructing matter, is used by a select few who are able to master the art. The rule of alchemy states that you cannot create something out of nothing, so when one wishes to obtain something, something of equal value must be paid. When the Elric brothers try to perform a human transmutation to bring their mother back from the dead, the experiment goes horribly wrong and they are left deformed with Ed losing an arm and a leg and Al losing his entire body, and having his soul put into an armored suit. The show follows Ed who has gained renown as the "Fullmetal Alchemist" who is on a quest to find out a way to get his brother and himself their bodies back.

Visuals: A *Besides the show involving elemental users that can manipulate matter, I think the artwork (not necessarily the character designs) for Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood and Avatar the Last Airbender are similar as well as the humor. It's a very colorful world with fluid animation and fantastic fight sequences. And like Avatar, characters are easy to distinguish from each other due to their characteristics like the Ishvalan having red eyes, Alphonse being a giant suit of armor, Edward being short with a metal arm and leg, the central military donning blue uniforms, and each of the Homunculi having their own monstrous forms and powers and the alchemists themselves having their own specialties with how they cast their alchemy.

Voice Acting: B *As usual, I watched the dub and throughout the series, I've gotten used to the few voices that did annoy me at first. Al's voice is super cute and I love him. Ed's voice is fine... when he's not yelling about someone calling him short. But the gag and the yelling grew on me in time especially as the gag gets used a bit less as the show gets more serious. But Ed is far from the only character that screams and gets angry out of nowhere for trivial things for no reason. I'm looking at you Winry! The "screaming for comedic effect" anime trope turned me off in season 1, but the show gets so much better with each season afterward. And most of the voices are really good.

Film Score/Soundtrack: In the context of the show, I felt like the music does a good job of enhancing scenes and being memorable. The themes that repeat in particular are excellent at this and during the many emotional moments during the show, that's where the score shines. However, as a standalone listen, I find the score to be pretty boring to listen to. There are a bunch of songs I hear and I'm like "oh I remember that, I like that one" but there's no way I could sit through a lot of the atmosphere fillers.

***My favorite track: Look, this is 5 seasons worth of material, there is no way I can only choose 1 song ok?

Requiem for the Blind Alchemist
(I am partial to bells and pretty melodies ok? This is a gorgeous song!)

Lurking
(You hear this too many times an episode to not include this eerie track amongst the best. It is a powerful atmosphere setter which is heavily used when important plot points are being discussed by the characters. It's a short and sweet song, but very, very memorable because it lingers)

Postlude
(Ditto to my first comment. I love songs that have bells. Haunting melodic lullabies I find memorable and really pretty)

***I can't find this last track and it's driving me NUTS!!! It's the "happy-sounding flute song" that plays in most episodes which serves as sort of a theme for Ed and Alphonse. I've searched for a long time but I am unable to figure out what to call it. So frustrating!

Characters:

Colonel Mustang is the GOAT. Master strategist underdog that finds a way out of the muck. Plus his flame alchemy is super powerful and I hate how underutilized it is.

Ling Yao started as a funny comedic relief and evolved into one of the best characters in the show.

Alphonse has awesome armor and his personality is so pure and I loved him!

Edward is probably the most likable whiny protagonist I've seen in a show. I love his determination, but he could be a bit much at times. And much like Mustang, he relies too much on hand-to-hand combat when he's a skilled alchemist and it drives me nuts.

Scar is like the Prince Zuko (see Avatar the Last Airbender) of Fullmetall but far more ruthless. He fights with a vengeance and eventually learns that revenge isn't the way of making the world a better place. But that doesn't mean that he doesn't kill his fair share of people either.

Johenheim has an awesome backstory and much like Mustang, he is someone you can't count out because the show likes to make you think he's going to lose when in actuality, he apparently was playing chess the entire time while the Dwarf in the Flask was playing checkers.

Homunculi:

1: Greed *Badass personality and voice. He just had a really cool vibe and I love how much of a wildcard he is. And when he fused to Ling Yao, game over. He already made a good first impression in his limited time in seasons 1 and 2, but then he solidified himself as my favorite Homunculi and one of my favorite characters on the show. "I want money, women, status, fame... and everything else in this world." In the end, he actually wanted friendship

2: Envy *The evilest of the Homunculi that committed the most amount of atrocities. He was a mass manipulator because of his ability to shape-shift into any form that he wished to. And besides that, he has a sharp tongue and has fun turning people on each other. Yet he still could hold his own in a fight because of how many souls he consumed. Envy was a parasite and a monster. But eventually we discover that Envy was jealous of humanity and needed humans as a vessel to survive because he hated his own ugly form.

3: Pride *Out of all of the Homunculi, Pride was the one with the most frightening ability. I almost wish he didn't reveal his identity to Hawkeye because he could have remained a secret and continued to cause a lot of problems for our heroes without them even knowing who was attacking them. Pride was the only Homunculus to share his Father's form and I find it ironic that his original body was of a human despite the Father's resentment to humanity and his desire to ascend to a more perfect being. Also, I loved when Kimblee stepped in to ensure that Pride didn't take Ed's body. That was badass!

4: Wrath *A friend of mine was telling me about a Kung Fu RPG game called Jade Empire and how in the game you can get a gun from a sidequest and that you can use it to kill the final boss because guns > Kung Fu to which I replied: that isn't the case in anime. In the world of Fullmetal Alchemist, somehow not only is Wrath's sword mightier than the gun, but it is mightier than the tank too. It was a bit absurd, but at the same time, awesome to see how many people were required to bring Wrath down. And it was beautifully ironic that Wrath died peacefully with a smile on his face

5: Lust *She was an interesting opponent for the time she was in the show. And much like Envy, I enjoyed it a lot when Mustang was able to unleash his power. Manipulation was her game and she did a number on Havoc and made Mustang's life a living hell.

6/7: Glutonny/Sloth *I lump these two together because outside of their main traits, they don't really have that much personality. Gluttony was always hungry and Sloth hated existing. Both could always be outsmarted by the heroes or manipulated by their fellow homunculi. And because of this, I always saw these two as minor players.

Cringeworthy Anime Moments: For a show with a premise as dark as this one has, it sure has a lot of light-hearted humor. Sometimes I like it, but it was often cringe-inducing. The loud girl squealing because she sees something she loves stereotype or the main character repeatedly getting pissed off when someone makes a joke to him, or the unrealistic use of violence as a means of characters interacting with each other all irritated the hell out of me as I watched this. But it does get significantly better after season 1 and I've actually grown to enjoy the humor for the most part even if my eyes roll when it happens.

Final Verdict: 9/10 *Fullmetal Alchemist is a ridiculously entertaining show with an awesome premise filled with lots of likable characters, awesome action sequences, entertaining villains, and a satisfying conclusion. Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood I've watched this anime 5 times now and I'm still fascinated by how much it can overwhelm with its execution and quality. In the shounen realm, it represents the pinnacle of quality that can be achieved and therefore has a solid reputation in the anime community. The focus was not to offer fans something that any other series can do but to create an entirely new experience. And that was excellently achieved here by removing most of the shounen clichés and keeping only minimal ones. Despite all the enthusiasm expressed and what's to come, I'm sadly disappointed by the anime adaptation afterfinishing the "Fullmetal Alchemist" manga last week. As many know, there are "2" different anime of the same name, from 2003 and 2009. The older series has almost nothing to do with the original and departs far from the manga. The newer series, on the other hand, follows the manga but made the mistake of deleting many scenes that were already in the old series. You notice less of this when you are completely drawn into the series. But once you have watched it several times, you will find gaps that are present in the narratives and sequences. After reading the manga, I have to agree that this is indeed the case. So much character screentime and relevant moments and dialogue have been removed so that the anime can maintain its tension. However, this caused many characters (especially Lust and Hughes) to lose a tremendous amount of sympathy by being much emptier shells in the anime than the characters they were capable of being in the manga. 
This breaks my heart, but by making these changes, you've lost a notable amount of potential for the series that could have elevated all the "Important and Shocking Moments" significantly more. 

So what does this series offer? 
A very original story of two brothers who broke the absolute taboo in the world of alchemy and had to reckon with huge consequences. The brother who lost his whole body and must live on as a suit of armor and the other who lost half his body. The impressive focus of the story is also due to the great will of the characters to want to achieve their goal, whereas in most works it seems more and more secondary, so here this remains constantly in the spotlight. On the journey of the siblings, they meet many bizarre characters, but also discover the "truth behind the truth" which was a very interesting approach. 
Especially important points here were the plot and the characters. 


[Story 10]

Most of the points that came off the manga were mostly character-related and showed the transition of many scenes. As for the plot, it is practically as polished here as in the manga. 
And especially here, I must note how positive the creativity and implementation of this plot are. Here an effort was made to create a small world, with an immensely gloomy and shocking background. 

As the story progresses, one learns more and more about the world and the many truths that lie within it. The roots of the military, the wars, and how far everything is intertwined. Constantly receiving new revelations that have always given the story a chance, the atmosphere has practically never collapsed. The tension was completely strained.
The finale, as expected, was weaker than the whole anime, but this is never surprising. Nonetheless, the final battle was well held and especially by the respective characters and their final confrontations. Since all the mysteries had already been solved by that point, all that remained was the final clash between two fronts. 

A very rare theme of alchemy, which was set as the main concept of the story, with respective approaches, principles, and philosophy. Like one of my favorites, the Equivalent Exchange approach. This was an excellent link in the narrative to highlight the importance of not rising above the laws of something people are only trying to understand anyway. Furthermore, alchemy was very interestingly eviscerated in this story, on different branches, perspectives, and applications. Comprehension, Deconstruction, Reconstruction, the pillars of the concept.


[Characters 8]

FMAB has many notable characters that I would say had fascinating personalities and excellent development. Unfortunately, some characters didn't get out of their diapers. Especially due to the lack of screen time, some particularly popular character deaths appeared, relatively mediocre for me. The implementation was good, no question about it. But a character who didn't even have 5 minutes of screen time will die accordingly. With more material and sympathy, her final moments could almost have been shocking, this chance was wasted.

So it would be far from saying the characters were flawless here.

However, some were very close due to various interactions, representations, and developments. Take, for example, the fascinating contrast between Ling and King Bradley, who were both who were destined to be number 11 (the eleventh prince and the eleventh candidate), both held/aspired to the same position and yet possessed such a fascinating contrast.

The 2 determined protagonists, Edward Elric and Alphonse. Although Alphonse looked like a boring character at first, he was the more mature and understanding of the two. No matter what emotions tormented him, he chose the passive and controlled way of coping with situations rather than cracking them with simple force. Whereas Edward, the smarter of the two, was very explosive due to his short temper. It is noteworthy, however, that the two did not benefit from a single, but from many different character traits and also had to adapt immensely depending on the situation.

Apart from that, there were characters like Roy Mustang, who had an immensely impressive final character arc. It was simple, but the representation of his goals, actions, and how they intersected just to achieve his personal goals was remarkable.
Scar has been very similar, also driven by revenge, he was one of the best characters in the series. With probably the greatest development.

Many supporting characters also received more or less positive attention. Notable ones like Kimbley, Hughes, Hawkeye, who had smaller character arcs, but still had enough influence on the series.

It is obvious, but the "7 sins" the "Homunculus" are the best representatives of the series and the most fascinating characters. Especially Envy, Bradley, Father, Greed. While Gluttony and Lust were also interesting, they lacked a massive amount of screen time. Which kept them relatively simple. Sloth, on the other hand, was relatively boring and had hardly any points worth mentioning.

Envy and Greed were both my personal favorites. Greed, the one who wanted everything and in the end achieved more than he could ever hope for. His development, and personality, was very nice.
Whereas Envy has been the perfect symbolic representation of human envy. He was the character who probably had the greatest influence on many scenes, as well as most of the whole story. And by far one of the best endings as an antagonist I've ever seen.

The author managed to give the symbolic sins so much depth and character that it still fascinates me to this day. As ironic as each of them came to an end.

Father and Hohenheim's character arc was also very interesting and how pathetic Father's attempts to understand humanity were. The symbolism behind his actions, his greed for knowledge and power, was still reflected, even after he had given up all of his sins.

You can interpret a lot in many of the characters and find a lot of fascinating little details regarding their existence and their irony, the role they were given.


[Animations 9]

Most of the animations are attractive and colorful. Through various adaptations to the respective scenes, the atmosphere could be raised by a certain play of colors. Especially later in the Brigs Tunnel, where it was most noticeable, in the depiction of light and darkness.

The fight animations fluctuated but were mostly very dynamic for individual scenes. Since the fights in the series are relatively short, it is all the better that the budget was placed correctly. Which also supported special moments of hype with beautifully choreographed movements.

[Music 10]

The outros have varied from pleasant to relaxing and beautiful. The musical style was more recognizable. But especially with the Osts, FMAB has by far some of the best intros you can find, each with its personal quality.

The Osts are beautiful too and I could hardly choose a favorite. They were very well laid out for various scenes and could support practically all kinds of moments. Whether emotional, mysterious or fascinating.



[Conclusion]

I would generally recommend the manga to every fan of this series if you want to have the same experience but again in full format. With more character screen time, better transitions, and no cut-out explanations. I was skeptical about it at the beginning, but I don't regret it, even if it damaged the image of the anime a bit.

Nonetheless, FMAB is one of the best anime I've ever seen, one of my personal favorites, and probably the best shounen to date. Even if you can argue about it, the quality and creativity of the author are undisputed.

First off, I'd like to start off by saying that FMAB is my first anime ever so bias is inevitable. However I will try to address the criticisms. Do note that while criticisms exist, they do not take away from my personal overall enjoyment of the series. Others might see it differently which is completely fine. I'm writing this review because lots of people in the anime community believe FMAB to be overrated. While I might not change your point of view, hopefully I can at least give you some reasons why some people (including myself) believe it to be one of the, if notthe best anime of all time. I don't think it is necessarily a masterpiece, nor is any anime, but I believe it be very close. Every anime has its flaws, that is inevitable. However, what makes something a good anime is how its highs outweigh its lows and how others perceive the flaws.

Story (9/10) FMAB is an anime packed with twists and turns, an incredible journey throughout its whole. It's written with such delicacy and care, and strings along the viewer. There's a strong aspect of mystery surrounding the homunculi (main villain group) and their origins but there's something that makes that mystery incredible. We are given bits of info at a time that lead us to make inferences. And then those inferences are proven to be not quite right-in fact what we are given is far more exciting than what we had imagined. We are never given too much exposition or lore at once but at the same time FMAB is always making us ask the questions. And thankfully, unlike some anime that raise questions and don't answer them, FMAB does the opposite. It'll answer questions and then bring new ones to the surface. Or partially answer them wanting us to crave for more. And when the big reveal finally arrives it is incredibly epic. Lots of people criticize the first arc as being rushed, but personally, I think it does exactly what it needs to. Lots of anime dwindle on the setting up the plot but FMAB gets right to the point and gives us 10-13 episodes of action packed goodness right off the bat. I will say however, the Briggs arc was far too slow. It introduced the worst villain (Sloth) and the plot slowed down from its previous pace. However, the briggs arc sets up an amazing final arc which I think makes up for it. The Final Arc is perfect. It flows so well from battle to battle that it all feels like one massive final battle. It's epic and militaristic filled to the brim with emotion and high stakes. It embodies the desperation of the Brother's improbable quest and the journey to the final segment. Finally, all the arcs flow very well. Everything is relevant and nothing is forgotten. The only episodes that are one offs are the two fillers. The story get progressively more hopeful as it continues. Additionally events in the the first arc very relevant in the final arc.

Art (10/10) Not much to say here. I'm not huge on animation in general in anime so long as it's not Ex-Arm or Berserk. The animation was great for its time and still looks great now. Particularly the homunculi regeneration animations were impressive. The chibi very much retains its manga style which pays homage to the manga and I believe enhances the experience. 

Sound/Music (10/10) The OST of FMAB fits perfectly. When it needs to be suspenseful the music is suspenseful, when it needs to be militarily grandiose it is epic, when it needs to be sad it is tragic. When listening to the OST on its own, you can even visualize the scenes that certain music is played in.

Character (10/10) This is definitely the most impressive aspect of FMAB. EVERY CHARACTER STAYS RELEVANT. Ed are not given too much power and require each other to balance one another. Ed is an alchemical genius but is lacking in combat. Al is vice versa. Together they are a strong duo but without each other they are limited. Ed in particular fights smarter, not harder. He doesn't sat some anime cliché when he loses like: "I wasn't strong enough" There is no boring training arc. He simply outsmarts the opponent when it is appropriate. He never wins a fight he shouldn't be able to win. The narrative digresses the focus from Ed and Al to all the side characters on several occasions.  They all matter in the grand scale of things and fit perfectly in the beautifully written work of art that is FMAB. For one, the female characters are given more justice than almost any shonen out there. They are strong willed and take the lead while still preserving their femininity. Winry doesn't need to be a hard ass. She is Ed's mechanic and yet she is given so much more than that. Olivia is FMAB's answer to the Damsel in Distress cliché. Characters are not one note. They are given multiple dimensions and each have their own unique philosophies that are complex. For example, Kimblee is a psychopath, but he also serves as a realist to put Ed and Al's outlandish goals into perspective. He values non hypocrisy and consistency, something that the narrative needs. The side characters are all so relevant and this is barely touching the surface of all the characters.

Enjoyment (10/10) If you couldn't already tell. I love this series more than is probably healthy. I enjoyed every second of it. FMAB is often critiqued for its comedy, especially in the first arc when it is the most dark. Often, people say that the comedy takes away from the dark moments. But I think it balances out the darkness, not making it too edgy.

Overall (10/10) If you're looking for an anime with an incredible story, fitting music, a balanced magic system, a unique shonen, epic moments, deep themes, an amazing journey, a classic that lives up to the hype, then I highly recommend giving brotherhood a shot. Episodes 1 and 27 are optional and the dub is phenomenal (arguably better than the sub, which is not common) The manga is also great and has some cut content the anime does not include. Enjoy!

The number one rated show on MyAnimeList. I mean as of writing the spot is held by Attack on Titan Season 4 Part 2, but it wouldn't surprise me if this show reclaims the number one spot in the long run. It honestly isn't my favourite show, but I can see the broad appeal and excellent quality. The first 10 episodes or so aren't that excellent frankly. They feel a bit rushed and I found them a bit boring personally. This is because they were speeding past this section of the manga, as it had been covered extensively by the original anime adaptation, Fullmetal Alchemist. Iunderstand why they did this, but it still would have been cool to see a properly fleshed out beginning of the story. But following this the show gets quite interesting, introducing new characters, motivations, information about the philosophers stone etc. This all culminates in the final arc. The ending arc is honestly peak television as people like to say, it's so damn good, and a nice length. Watching the kinda boring first episodes definitely pays off at the end, no doubt.

The character development is so damn good. It's fairly generic in a sense, but it's done so damn well. My personal favourite character would be Colonel Mustang, such a damn legend. I prefer this interpretation of him over the interpretation in the original anime adaptation actually. I like the dark side of him and how it's explored. But of course the ambition, grit and wit present in his character is so damn badass.

Whilst the show is often light-hearted, the exploration of deep themes such as war, peace, genocide etc. are some of the best factors of the show. I think Avatar the Last Airbender is similar in this regard, with both shows grappling with ethnic groups that were both brought to near extinction. The character Scar is of this ethnic group, from the nation of Ishval, and his character arc is really good. It could be argued that these themes have fairly generic feel good liberal conclusions (in the broad enlightenment sense not the left wing sense), but I still think the explorations are interesting regardless.

For a better beginning arc I think it's worth watching the original Fullmetal Alchemist adaptation before this one, but if 115 episodes of anime sound like too much I think you should just stick to this one.

The humour is criticized sometimes on the show. But I think it's mildly amusing and works well. Nothing laugh out loud but it keeps a degree of comic relief to the show and some occasionally hilarious moments. I like the recurring gag Edward does where he puts short jokes into other people's mouths and being angry at them.

I didn't care much for the opening and closing songs initially, but they've grown on me, I think they're quite solid.

There are a lot more things to discuss about this show but I'm sure other reviews have covered that well enough. It's clear that this show is a classic, and considered by many to be a masterpiece. The spot it holds in Otaku's hearts is valid in my view, I give it a 9/10.

Context: This was one of the first shows I watched, so I am naturally gonna be biased a bit positive throughout this, do keep that in mind. Story: FMA:B is a relatively simple story, a classic adventure plot, with a bit of mystery thrown in (albeit one that resolves itself long before the show ends). However, what it lacks in insane depth and complexity, it makes up for in execution. Every single plot thread that gets brought up, pays off, most of them even coming in right to the end of the 64-episode run. No scene feels wasted, but equally, you don't have to be keeping notes ofevery little event just to understand what's going on. It finds the sweet spot for flashing back, where it does it enough to remind you of what you need to know, but not so much as to become annoying. 

Art:

Visually this show is perfectly passable. Nothing ever looks particularly terrible in motion, save a few moments where they get a bit...pain. But equally nothing is ever particularly jaw droppingly pretty. Equally, it being a show from 2009, it has a few attempts of what look like CG. They're again, mostly ok, but do occasionally grate a bit. The art does not ever detract from the rest of the show however, which is the most important part.

Sound:

First and foremost, this soundtrack is a gift from God. Akira Senju knocked it out of the park with this piece of work. The sound effects are, as all good sound work is, unnoticeable, with one glaring exception. There's one instant where for reasons unbeknownst to man or god, all ambiance cuts out to have a man sipping tea in total silence. And the dub (yes, yes, hang draw and quarter me for watching dubs) is wonderful with all the actors giving top tier performances. 

Characters:

This is again an area where FMA shines through. It has a wide cast of characters, and yet each and every one of them feels deep, developed, and for use of a better word, alive. Even those who turn up only briefly, like General Grumman, have well fleshed out personalities. It's one of the few shows where nearly every death, for heroes and villains alike, brings a tear to my eye.

Enjoyment:

Yeah, this show is fun, in case you hadn't got that already. It can bounce seamlessly between laugh-out-loud comedy, brutally enticing action scenes and heartwrenching emotional moments, and everyone already knows this. It's a show that I'd heartily recommend to anyone who hasn't seen it, and even those who have should give it a re-watch. 

Overall: 

FMA: Brotherhood is one of my favourite shows, one that I keep coming back to, and one that inspired me to actually make an account on this site, to start cataloguing and see if I can't find a show as good as it. Watch it if you haven't, watch it again if you have.

Hi, this is my first review, I hope it's good... Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is an extremely highly rated show. It has been the #1 highest rated show on MAL for over a decade. It's the 3rd most popular anime as of today. But does it live up to the hype? Yes. It absolutely does. But before I review this series I must reveal some biases I might have. This was the first anime I ever watched (outside of Pokémon), and I haven't watched a lot of anime (I've only been watching for about 3 months), so I didn't really have any other anime to compare it to.Secondly, I haven't seen the 2003 series, though I have heard a lot about it.

Now, on to the review:

STORY: 9/10

Brotherhoods story was great. The plot is concise, easily understandable, and has one of the most satifying conclusions in any media, ever. The pacing was a little off for the first 12 or so episodes (because that was already covered in the '03 version), but it definitely picks up the slack at the masterpiece that is episode 19. For the rest of the series, the pacing is on point, with diverse locals, mysteries of alchemy and goverment conspiricies.

CHARACTERS: 10/10

I think I can still name a COUPLE DOZEN characters from this series and say a little about them. These are some of the most memorable characters I've ever seen. Edward is great protagonist, and Alphonse bounces off of him quite nicely. The ''Edward is short'' joke got a little (haha) old eventually, but it pops up less often further into the series. Roy Mustang is badass, Hawkeye is also really cool. The main villians all have entertaining personalities, and you can even sympathise with some of them. The character development was also amazing.

ANIMATION: 10/10

This show was made by Studio Bones, so this rating shouldn't come as a surprise to anybody. This show has some of the best fights I've ever seen. Character designs were all memorable and the world looked awesome.

SOUND: 9/10

The opening were all bangers (especially the first one), and even some of the endings were bops. This show has ONE OF THE BEST DUBS EVER, and it's hard the top the voice acting in the sub, so that's saying something. The music used in the show was good, but I didn't remember a lot of it.

ENJOYMENT: 10/10

This show had me HOOKED. I loved each and every episode (except the recap, that episode was okay), and I watched the last 9 episodes of the show in one day (that's a 
lot for me). I couldn't shut up about this anime when I was talking to other people either, much to their dismay.

OVERALL: 9.6/10 (Rounded out to a 10/10)

This show is amazing, and if you haven't seen it yet, DROP ANYTHING YOU'RE DOING RIGHT NOW AND WATCH IT. The flaws are so minor, you might as well call them nitpicks. So, I can't feasibly give this show anything lower than a 10.

I will preface this by saying I am very VERY biased. I feel the original story was better. The original ending was far more resonating. Here is my reasoning, the original was far more tragic and was more fitting for the context of the entire anime. The whole anime is about the tragic events that lead up to that end. And it emphasizesequivalent exchange as it is intended. I absolutely LOVE that Edward had to give up his body for Alphonse to get his back. Winrey never got to tell Ed she loved him. So many tragedies that shows the viewer that not everything comes out like the movies. Not everything gets a happy ending. 

What I DIDNT like about the original is that they left the window open for Ed to return to his world. It would've been better if he was permanently trapped in our version of earth. The emphasis needs to be that he can never go back. Ed and Al played god, and they got punished for it. To give Ed the ability to return to his own earth deminishes that punishment completely. 

FMA: Brotherhood is a bastardization of that story to please some critics that couldnt deal with an ending that wasnt very "disney like." Ed lives and gets to marry Winrey. Alphonse gets his body back. Al still hates milk. Its all happy ending horseshit. 

The only positives I have to say about this version is the addition of Olivier Mira Armstrong. She is BOSS! And, it never gets more badass than Col. Roy "muthaf'in" Mustang. When he snaps King Bradley to crispy goodness, I had a nerdgasm. That was hot fire!

Overall, FMA: Brotherhood is a good anime. It does deserve to be treated as one of the best anime to ever be made. But calling it a masterpiece is a fallacy. And that is one of the absolute WORST things about Myanimelist is the amount of trend followers that sometimes frequent here. But this anime doesnt deserve first place. At least in my opinion, Cowboy Bebop should be #1. Not this anime. FMA: Brotherhood is a great anime, just not a masterpiece and a little overrated.

Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is one of the highest rated anime of all time, and as someone who finished the series I can see why. Real stakes, real characters, and real fun. I've been excited to write this review for a while, so let's get into those juicy details. Story (9): The story of FMAB is very coherent and I was never once confused during the story. They expanded upon the universe and each of the important characters very well, and they always did a good job of weaving each of the arcs together. As someone who never watched the original Fullmetal Alchemist, I was surprised that Iwas never lost in the story besides the first few minutes of the first episode. All of the arcs were exciting to varying degrees, with the most 'boring' arc being just a 7 from me. The story kept getting better and better with each episode, which only made me more excited to keep watching. I can't talk about the detail of the ending, but it was really amazing and definitely worth the journey. 

Art (9):
The artwork for this series is great. The metallic colors and shades as well as the duller pastels really added to the more serious tone of this anime. FMAB does have some comedy moments, but the art style perfectly represents what it was going for; a more series anime that wants to make you FEEL the stakes. The artwork and colors do a great job of reminding us of the intents and purposes of this anime. 

Sound (7):
The sound for this series was really good and did what it was supposed to do, but it wasn't anything too special. I noticed the sound, such as metal clanking or gunfire or Alchemical noise, and it always fit the occasion and did a good job of drawing attention to what was happening on the screen, but I was never like "woah that's some awesome sound" I was more like "this is good, but I am too focused on the art to notice this". 

Characters (10):
The characters in this anime are really perfect. I always either felt a strong attachment and relatability to the struggles of some of the "good guys" like Edward or absolutely despised the "bad guys" of this anime. I really like how even with the "bad guys" of the series I actually was able to understand WHY they were doing the things they were, which made them relatable in a way too. This is something many series miss out on that FMAB really did well. I could understand the goals of every character in this anime, which made it all the more investing. 

Enjoyment (10):
As I think I mentioned earlier, this series kept getting more and more exciting with every episode. Each arc seemed to improve from the previous one, with the exception of a couple moments that felt a little off for me. Nevertheless, I still enjoyed this series as a 10 despite its flaws because I understood what it was going for and that happened to be something that is right up my alley. 

Overall (10):
If you like lighthearted series, you probably won't like FMAB. This series is more serious than most anime around, and while it does work in its favor, I realize that's not for everyone. If you love high stakes, intensity, and sometimes even a feeling of powerlessness followed by overcoming all odds, you'll probably like this series. Don't let me choose your path though, if you want to watch it, just go for it. You can always drop it later if you don't like it, but I think you'll probably enjoy it, but if you don't, well, I am sorry.

Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood held the #1 spot on MAL for years until it was overtaken by Frieren. It is over 15 years old. Does it still hold up? Short answer is yes. Absolutely! I will focus on the themes of the series over the technical stuff as that seems to be covered already by others. Two brothers committed taboo when they were young, trying to bring their mother back to life, but it backfired and one brother lost his body, while the other lost an arm and a leg. Together, the brothers vow to fix their mistakes and get their bodies back. It is a greatshow with timeless messages, especially on going too far with science to the point where it becomes objectively wrong. The main characters are also made to confront their own beliefs and face their shortcomings. Throughout the show, the brothers learn that science cannot solve every problem, nor can it explain everything, such as the human soul or life in general. For example, there is a scene where the brothers witness the birth of a newborn baby. They realize that scientific explanations can never truly make the natural creation of new life any less miraculous. Moreover, science cannot explain human emotions, such as love, and the complexities of the human person cannot be understood by algorithms and lists of materials. This leads to another theme throughout the series about the dangers of playing God. It criticizes those who wish to be masters over nature, life, and death—those with a lust for forbidden knowledge who use science to build metaphorical Towers of Babel. It shows the horrors that unchecked scientific advancement can lead to, such as more inhumane, brutal warfare, human experimentation, justification for imperialism, loss of objective moral standards, loss of humanity, etc. After a discovery is made, men often use this knowledge to further selfish agendas and commit attrocities. The show also explores themes like what it means to be human, the importance of community, human connection, man’s relationship with the world around him, the necessity of sacrifice to achieve goals and become better, the power of kindness and friendship, breaking out of the cycle of hate and violence, forgiveness and redemption, life’s challenges, and the never-ending pursuit of truth.

The characters are also very well-developed. They are all forced to come to terms with realities that they would rather not face. Some experience guilt for the things they did, things they didn't do, and things they could do, but have not yet done, while others face difficult truths they do not want to believe. By the end, every character is different from who they were at the beginning. 

It's a great show with timeless messages and great storytelling. It has the perfect balance of action, comedy, philosophy, social critique, and character development. If there is any anime show out there that can be enjoyed by practically anyone, it is this show (although the animation has not aged too well). 


Is this show still one of the best anime series ever made? Absolutely! Do yourself a favor and watch it. You will not regret it.
