A doctor warns them it's "The Devil's research" if they try to find out how to make it. Don't wanna give too much away but this show isn't afraid to get dark, because earlyon.. it gets messed up real fast. It's still a good show, Edward is still trying to work through his trauma.. slowly but surely! Lot of the characters are cool, Ling being my most favorite. The fight scenes are amazing and I love the comedy! If you don't mind a show to go from 0 to 100 then FMA:B is up your alley.

More than a decade later and its still the king the medium. The plot takes its time and thinly distributes over each episode but uses that time to develop its characters and environment. It is an optimal pacing. You'll find yourself asking questions each episode. The anime just gives you the answers 10 episodes later which can be critiqued writing wise but it is still engaging. It isn't immature compared to most shounen but doesn't take its self too seriously either which helps the tone. The humor doesn't always land but it does when it needs to. It has consistent central themes of war, politics, andfamily that are explored to give the series its depth. 
The characters become endearing overtime especially Al. 

The fight scenes are more like problems the protags solve rather than the common combat simulation of who dies first. A bit like jojo. Often solved with magic which brings me to my critique:

Although this is a magic based show, I feel like the magic could be better explained. It claims to have rules but I don't think the rules are really consistent. Like sometimes the protags come across a similar problem that they solved before. For example edward can fix a radio when its completely in pieces but cant fix his prosthesis when it breaks. Like it or not but it seems to be a very much a power level based magic despite how much the show claims it isn't. All the characters have limits on how much raw plot usefulness they can do with their magic but it isnt really clear what exactly those limits are. Then you'll have characters that are OP when they need to be like Roy Mustang that thanos snaps shit with his flames. Thats my only criticism really. Quite a big flaw but doesn't take away from the enjoyment.

Short Review: (minor spoilers) A great anime indeed. Stable quality throughout, thematically consistent (mostly) from start to finish. In comparison, some classics I was obsessed with in my childhood are full of retconned elements (Saint Seiya, Fist of the North Star, etc.). When the actions start to get going, the show is usually a total blast. A few things held it back from perfection for me though, namely, immersion-breaking gags; wishful-thinking resolutions for some core antagonists and a not-so-subtle anti-male ideology (to be fair many anime sport "goddess-dominating-over-men" trope, but this issue sticks out in FMAB's otherwise amazing writing for me). Sorry FMAB fans and MAL,but in my opinion there are more stellar shonen/seinen shows. 

For clarifications, I never read the FMA manga, nor have I seen the 2003 anime version. I went into FMAB only knowing the basic premise--that two brothers paid a great price after a transmutation attempted for resurrecting their mom went horribly wrong. On MAL, the show might just permanently occupy the throne of the best rated anime ever. I never hated or resented that (just as being an IMDB user and casual reviewer for years, I've never had a problem with Shawshank Redemption permanently being No.1, despite it's never my favorite movie). Some of my friends shunned MAL for this reason (to quote a friend, "the rating system on MAL can only give you an idea of the most popular shows, but not really the best shows"). I want to give the top shows here a fair chance, and I am glad to see different views from people here. That said, I started FMAB with my expectations cautiously cranked to 9.5/10. When I finished the last episode, I was happy that the show mostly lives up to the hype, mostly.

Pros: 

+ Overall a fantastic production. Very consistent quality. As a fantasy/action/adventure/military-themed shonen/seinen that dishes out supernatural combat in spades, the show is surprisingly grounded and gripping. Almost on the level of Hunter X Hunter for me (close but not). 

+ Sustained suspense. Around half-way, the show becomes easy to binge in a single sitting. Most episodes ends on an intriguing cliffhanger. 

+ Overall story and themes. A very straight-forward take on modern humanism among other heavy subject matters (Fascism, Scientism, Existentialism, Utilitarianism vs. Moralism, etc.). Again the show shines in its consistency in its treatment of these matters. The entire anime has only one single arc from start to finish (mostly driven by the dual protagonists' quest to get their bodies back).

+ Art and animation. I am sure the design for Envy's true form alone deserves some kind of award. It's one of the best examples of blending 3d and 2d elements in an anime. Butter-smooth explosions and special effects. Characters have their distinct designs (unlike some popular shows that keep copying and pasting the same face on characters). 

+ Endearing characters and their suitable fates. For example, the major twist regarding the protagonists' father is layered and smart, and a clear testament to the talent of the writer/author. Von's ending could have easily been generic (but still proper), yet the author was able to put extra thought into it. Same thing goes with King Bradley, Dr. Marco and Scar. 

Cons: 

- The show seems to be shy/unconfident for being serious and brutal, therefore inserting countless chibi-character sequences, sometimes at the cost of the immersion/thrills (e.g. during some of the most intense and white-knuckled battles the main characters suddenly turned chibi for gags, and the enemies just stopped attacking). I am not 100% against comic relief or gags during intense/mature sequences, but I'd prefer that they don't break my immersion. 

- For a show about demonic forces and their real consequences on humanity, the author went for a wishful-thinking, naïve conclusion for some of the main antagonists (e.g. a certain deadly sin's turn of heart and final sacrifice as he was "transformed" after taking over another character's body). This problem, in my opinion, undermines the show's overall believability and the weight of the Xerxes incident (if the lesson Von learned at Xerxes is "don't let the devil play with your seemingly innocent wishes and desires, for the devil never plays fair", he should never had led his sons onto the path of Alchemy, but then again there wouldn't have been this story at all). All the serious explorations of morality/metaphysical aspects before the climax/ending were also weakened for this reason. 

- Anti-male imagery dominates the show. I lost count how many times our male heroes were casually bullied or beaten up by super-powered, dominating and sneering female characters. A main villain is just named "Father". A most masculine character has the head of a baby, and often soils himself at the mere sight of his ultra-tough sister. The ideal "family man" is really just a bubbling idiot who shows off his happy family around (causing dire consequences for himself). By the examples of some characters (e.g. Col. Mustang; Lt. Hawkeye; King Bradley), the author is very capable of writing layered, nuanced and realistic characters. Therefore it puzzles me why she couldn't write more strong female characters who don't need to assert their independence, prowess and dignity by beating men into pulps. To be fair there are other exaggerated representations of this type of "girl power" in many other anime, but for FMAB's overall amazing writing, this issue sticks out like a sore thumb for me. 

- Some uninteresting side stories and slow-to-a-halt episodes. Like I said, when the actions start, the show is usually a total blast. There are also quality quiet character moments, but some episodes made me just want to fast-forward. For a large portion of the final climax, Edward as the central character was just given generic brainless zombie-like creatures to fight with. Moments like this made me shout in my thought: "come on, FMAB, you can do much better than this!"

In conclusion, Fullmetal Alchemist Brotherhood is a great show with some caveats. 
Baseline quality: 9/10; in the end a strong 8.4/10 due to the issues mentioned.

First of all, I have seen the original FMA and although it was very popular and original, the pacing and conclusion did not sit too well with me. Brotherhood is meant to be a remake of the original, this time sticking to the manga all the way through, but there were people who thought it would spoil the franchise. That myth should be dispelled, as there's only one word to describe this series - EPIC. I admit that as I've seen the original and read the manga, the pacing of Brotherhood seems to start off being VERY fast (I finally got used to the pacing afterwatching the first fifteen eps or so). Events that took up half a volume of the manga and had spread though a few episodes of the original anime were now shown in just a single episode. However, after trying to look at it from the perspective of someone who's new to FMA (not comparing it to the manga nor the original), I believe that the pacing works and it manages to tell an intriguing story effectively with little confusion. The plot is full of clever ideas and unpredictable twists that link various parts of the story together. By the final episode, all loose ends are neatly tied up and what's left is a hugely satisfying epilogue.

The animation in FMA Brotherhood is crisp and very well done (although it does sometimes dip a bit in quality). Compared to the original FMA it's a bit simpler but that's just because the original set a very high standard to follow. The facial emotions of the characters are also perfectly presented. The action scenes are brilliant and VERY well animated, with a variety of alchemy techniques and other talents being displayed nearly every episode. The various battles are consistently exciting to watch, but somehow get even better towards the end of the series.

The voice acting is of an excellent and consistent quality, and I think that pretty much all the characters have voice actors which suit their personalities. The majority of the openings/endings are a pleasure to watch due to fantastic animated sequences and theme songs. The background music which play during the episodes usually fit very well with the situation, although some tracks seem to be overused a little at first. This becomes less of a problem as the series progresses, with plenty of new music being introduced to support the story as it reaches the finale.

Moving on to the characters (best thing about this series), the original FMA focussed mainly on Ed and Al and on their struggles to regain their bodies, whereas Brotherhood also explores other characters to great detail at the same time. The majority of the spotlight is still on the two brothers, but it highlights their interactions with new characters which were not present in the original anime. New characters include a group of people from Xing (a neighbouring country), another person from the Armstrong family (who I think has become one of the coolest members of the supporting cast), and a new main antagonist. For me, the Xingese characters in particular (Ling Yao and Mei Chang among others) provide a new dimension to the FMA world, by showing us a different culture to the militaristic one we're familiar with. I think the new antagonist is an improvement on the original FMA, as this person has a much stronger and clever link to the Elric brothers' father. Returning characters from the original FMA, such as Mustang and Scar, are much more awesome and developed due to the fact that Brotherhood is 100% faithful to the manga. Plus, Winry Rockbell now has a much more active role in the story. I can say for sure that this anime has one of the best main/supporting casts I've ever seen, and you'd probably find it difficult to label any of the recurring characters (whether they are good or evil) as being either boring or unnecessary in terms of the storyline.

One of the many good things about this series is that there has been absolutely no filler at all (yes, I'm thinking of Naruto, Inuyasha, etc), which prevents the story from losing momentum. All the episodes are concise and every scene is important as part of the huge plot. The dialogue fully explains everything and is straight to the point. As multiple characters are explored there are lots of side stories, but these are all perfectly intertwined with the main story of the Elric brothers and more often than not directly influence their journey too. Like most anime series, there are things from the manga which have been left out, but these are usually just restricted to comedy moments. There has been one episode which shows a lot of flashbacks of events so far, but that's forgiven as it shows the most epic moments of the series, and also provided us with some history on the father of the Elric brothers.

FMA Brotherhood will be sorely missed now that it's finished. It is excellent in every aspect and has very little, if anything, that can be called a flaw (maybe rushed character development at first due to the fast pacing, but this quickly subsides). Each episode feels like it's too short, a testimony to how much it draws you in to the story and characters. There are moments which leave you smiling, laughing, sad and simply amazed. Try this anime, it's recommended for absolutely everyone, to newcomers and to those familiar with Fullmetal Alchemist.

At first, I though this show was very slow and wasn't going anywhere. But then once I started season 2, I thought it was one of the best shows, not only anime, but SHOWS of all time. Then I continued watching, and now that i am done, i can say it is the second best show I have ever seen. ( breaking bad is no.1). The story is a masterpiece, and you cant help but love all of the characters. ( except May Chang, she was annoying. Here are all my individual points Story: 10. story was possibly the best story of any anime everwritten, due to the amazing plot twist and outstanding dialogue. Amazing backstory for the Elric brothers as, well, giving a very sad and heart wrenching story for the brothers.

Art: 9. The art for this was outstanding. It also has a very unique character design, not using the traditional pointy chins and instead using round heads and big eyes. The characters are not sexualized, which is a bad thing for some people but i prefer the characters to super sexualized because it is uncomfortable to watch. The animation and fights were also very clean and fluid.

Sound: 10. The music in this show was outstanding. Every opening was top tier, especially " hologram" and "again". The soundtrack was equally amazing, from the eerie music of the homunculus, to the upbeat music in the battles. It was a perfect soundtrack from end to beginning. 

Characters: 10. The characters in this show were impeccable and probably the best supporting characters of all time. From the military characters ( King Bradley, 
Roy Mustang, Riza Hawkeye, Jean Havoc, and Olivier and Alex Armstrong), The Homunculi, ( Wrath, Gluttony, Pride, Greed, Lust, Envy, and Sloth), the main characters ( Edward, Alphonse, Scar, Kimblee, Winry, Ling, The chimeras, Izumi Curtis, Hoenheim, lan Fan, Maes Hughes, Dr marcoh etc...) As you can see, there is a whole cast of amazing characters in this show.

Ending: 10. The most perfect ending in television history. Period. Everything wraps up in a tear-jerking, heartfelt, amazing ending that needs to be studied by future anime writers for years to come. I can not give this anime enough praise and fully deserves the no.1 spot on this website.

Story The story was told by providing a lot of context for why things are the way they are. As an example, show why Alphonse is wearing armor and how Edward lost an arm and a leg. There was a really nice sequence of events leading up to the show's end. To me, the story was quite unique. A lot of stuff in the show was very unbiased. They stayed neutral. They follow only one rule. If you want to gain something you must lose something in return. An equal exchange. Don't worry, there was some comedic humor sprinkled throughout, but they never lost sight of thestory.

They are some mysteries that got me thinking a lot about how things are in the show. And why did this person perish while the other did not? It took a lot of thought. As I previously stated, they provide a lot of background information. Some flashbacks as to why things are. Those flashbacks were much needed.

Art
The animation looks very very good. They use CGI extensively, but only for a large number of people and objects required for the story. The fighting scene animation was really fluid. The distinct character design ties the story together. They were some characters who looked alike, but it didn't bother me.

Sound
I wish Edward and Alphonse's voices had gotten deeper as they grew older. It was kind of weird to hear a child-like voice in a grown man's body. The background music complements the story. The orchestral sound for the sad scene only added to the sadness.

Character
Edward was a well-rounded individual. He uses his knowledge of alchemy to try to reclaim his mother and to save his country. He does have a temper whenever someone calls him short or anything that relates to something being small. He dislikes it when people's lives are taken away. He doesn't care how long it takes. He doesn't want to take a life of a human being. He grew quite a bit simply through experience. 

Alphonse is also a well-rounded individual. He can keep his cool better than his older brother, Edward. He, too, employs alchemy. Just like his brother. He thinks similarly to his brother. Doesn't enjoy killing.

All the antagonists/villains did have the motivation and they're all the same. I don't have much to say because their motivation is the most important aspect of the story. Without that this show would've been useless. So that being said the villains did carry the show. The story had no narrator. I like Edward Elric but not King Bradley. But I'll never forget Edward's long blonde hair.

Enjoyment
Others, I believe, would enjoy this show. There are enough episodes to complete the story. I'll probably watch it again. Just for the mystery, because I enjoy thinking. But I might only watch the climax area to the resolution. This was really a memorable show.

This is a fantastic adaption of the manga storyline. When it comes to writing about large topics inside tiny tales, Arakawa is a master. Fullmetal Alchemist is, at its heart, a narrative of two brothers who are learning to mourn and grow up together. The serious topics of what it means to be alive in life beyond death are handled delicately and expertly subverted throughout the show. The program's type of alchemy is used often enough to make it a wonderful action show, but it does not get in the way of the plot, which is excellent. The plot and the characters are the onesthat have the power in the program, not the other way around. This is an excellent anime for anyone who is interested in topics about their purpose in life as well as the hereafter. 

A recurring topic in the program, grief, is not overplayed or pounded to death (haha). There are many humorous moments in the program, and the characters who are presented in the anime are so well-written that we, as viewers, get emotionally concerned in the fate of each character.

Some of the show's disadvantages, on the other hand, include the fact that the surface plots get complicated. In addition, the explanation and application of alchemy in the program might be a little unclear at times. However, one positive aspect of the writing is that the people and their adventures are depicted so beautifully that the confused power relations may be overlooked. Overall, this is a fantastic program that serves as an excellent introduction for those who wish to watch more serious anime.

As i'm sure you already know, FMAB is an anime that is known both to anime watchers and non-anime watchers. It has dominated the polls, taking the spot of greatest anime of all time, but does it deserve that title? Let's look and see. Story: 10/10 The story itself is rather straightforward. You have Edward and Alphonse Elric, two boys who lost their mother and attempted to use alchemy to revive her. Unaware of the basic principle that encompasses alchemy - The law of equivalent exchange - Ed and Al end up losing their arm, leg, and whole body, respectively. The boys build their notoriety astop-class alchemists and come across other characters with which the story goes into more depth as they face a threat that could destroy them all. Despite the anime's straightforward approach, Fullmetal Alchemist does an amazing job of fleshing out each character and the world around them, something that the original FMA does not do very well. A testament to this would be the introduction of the people of Xing and the development of characters like the Fuhrer and side characters like Jerso. To add on to this, unlike the original FMA, this anime is faithful to the original manga and paces it very well. The show itself doesn't feel too long or too short; It's just the right length. The worldbuilding and lore are top-tier, touching on subjects like the Ishvalan War and the after-effects of it, which serve as one of the main driving forces in the story.

Art: 10/10

Bones Animation did a great job of animating the series. I don't have much to say about this. Even the animation for the openings was absolutely amazing, the first two openings in particular.

Sound: 7/10

Despite the amazing storytelling, i believe it does fall short on the OST side of things. There were a few soundtracks that would stick with me and others that i'd just forget about. The openings, however, were amazing and well-chosen. The voice actors were spectacular as well. Romi Park and Rie Kugimiya do a wonderful job portraying Ed and Al,  and don't get me started on the Fuhrer and Greed's voice actors. Overall, the cast was amazing and brought more life to the anime, offsetting the "good but not great" soundtrack.

Characters: 10/10

The best thing about the series. The original series had more focus on our two main characters, Ed and Al, which isn't necessarily bad. With that being said, I appreciate when stories touch on the main character's surroundings and give you a more thorough understanding of the climate they live in, and Brotherhood exceeds my expectations in that regard. The introduction of the characters from the fictional country of Xing, to seeing the most irrelevant side characters have some sort of role to play. It outdoes it's predecessor in terms of fleshed out characters. Some series have characters that you can't seem to like, but with FMAB, even the most rotten individual is well written. I mean, have you seen how many FMAB fans talk about how great a person Shou Tucker is....?

Enjoyment: 9/10

As you've probably seen (assuming you've read up until this point) I've had nothing but good things to say about this series. It's a very enjoyable series, but the fast pacing might take a bit of getting used to. When i was watching it, I got used to it about 5 episodes in but some people would take about 15 episodes before they got hooked. Each person is different but once you're hooked, you will enjoy it.

Overall: 9/10 

FMAB is an amazing series, especially for those that are trying to get into the anime scene. It's one that I've recommended to friends of mine, both anime and non-anime watchers, and is a great starting point for anyone trying to take a dip into the wide sea that is the anime scene. Don't even watch the original FMA release, if you want it as it was released in the manga, watch FMAB. You will not regret it. :)

this is probably my favorite anime. i'll preface this by saying i havent watched the original FMA anime (yet) so i cannot compare and instead just gonna focus solely on FMAB itself. FMAB has a really good plot. it certainly has its ups and downs but id say it's still consistently good until things get a little out of hand in the final part of the story. the world building is phenomenal, alchemy is nicely explained without going in too deep (*cough* hxh nen). the world is very interesting and while the plot is always good enough to stay in one place for a goodamount of time, it makes you want to see more of the worlds diversity all the time. 
again, its not all great and theres a bunch of unnecessary scenes as well as the dumbass "meme animations" (for a lack of a better word) in between. while i can easily live with some scenes that dont contribute anything to the plot, the caricaturesque scenes just make me cringe. it's not even remotely funny and it's hugely annoying if they keep repeating the same terrible jokes and memes over and over. the series has a lot of positivity and heartfelt moments in between a rather dark main plot. it wasnt at all necessary to try and "lighten up the mood" - if anything it destroyed the suspense and the "feel" there was to the show.

Moving on to the art i think the art is mostly brilliant. the fighting scenes arent the only aspect that makes the series shine in this category, the facial expressions, background etc. all look really nice. if youve watched the series and read my review so far you already know what i didnt like: yea the meme-cringe-scenes and their terrible artwork. moving on.

The sound is the only part of the series where id give a full 10/10. aside from one OP i think theyre all nothing short of amazing. the endings are great as well and i liked the voice acting, too. no complaints here - to be fair: judging the music is rather subjective.

The animation in FMA Brotherhood is crisp and very well done (although it does sometimes dip a bit in quality). Compared to the original FMA it's a bit simpler but that's just because the original set a very high standard to follow. The facial emotions of the characters are also perfectly presented. The action scenes are brilliant and VERY well animated, with a variety of alchemy techniques and other talents being displayed nearly every episode. The various battles are consistently exciting to watch, but somehow get even better towards the end of the series. The voice acting is of an excellent and consistent quality, and Ithink that pretty much all the characters have voice actors which suit their personalities. The majority of the openings/endings are a pleasure to watch due to fantastic animated sequences and theme songs. The background music which play during the episodes usually fit very well with the situation, although some tracks seem to be overused a little at first. This becomes less of a problem as the series progresses, with plenty of new music being introduced to support the story as it reaches the finale.

Moving on to the characters (best thing about this series), the original FMA focussed mainly on Ed and Al and on their struggles to regain their bodies, whereas Brotherhood also explores other characters to great detail at the same time. The majority of the spotlight is still on the two brothers, but it highlights their interactions with new characters which were not present in the original anime. New characters include a group of people from Xing (a neighbouring country), another person from the Armstrong family (who I think has become one of the coolest members of the supporting cast), and a new main antagonist. For me, the Xingese characters in particular (Ling Yao and Mei Chang among others) provide a new dimension to the FMA world, by showing us a different culture to the militaristic one we're familiar with. I think the new antagonist is an improvement on the original FMA, as this person has a much stronger and clever link to the Elric brothers' father. Returning characters from the original FMA, such as Mustang and Scar, are much more awesome and developed due to the fact that Brotherhood is 100% faithful to the manga. Plus, Winry Rockbell now has a much more active role in the story. I can say for sure that this anime has one of the best main/supporting casts I've ever seen, and you'd probably find it difficult to label any of the recurring characters (whether they are good or evil) as being either boring or unnecessary in terms of the storyline.

One of the many good things about this series is that there has been absolutely no filler at all (yes, I'm thinking of Naruto, Inuyasha, etc), which prevents the story from losing momentum. All the episodes are concise and every scene is important as part of the huge plot. The dialogue fully explains everything and is straight to the point. As multiple characters are explored there are lots of side stories, but these are all perfectly intertwined with the main story of the Elric brothers and more often than not directly influence their journey too. Like most anime series, there are things from the manga which have been left out, but these are usually just restricted to comedy moments. There has been one episode which shows a lot of flashbacks of events so far, but that's forgiven as it shows the most epic moments of the series, and also provided us with some history on the father of the Elric brothers.

FMA Brotherhood will be sorely missed now that it's finished. It is excellent in every aspect and has very little, if anything, that can be called a flaw (maybe rushed character development at first due to the fast pacing, but this quickly subsides). Each episode feels like it's too short, a testimony to how much it draws you in to the story and characters. There are moments which leave you smiling, laughing, sad and simply amazed. Try this anime, it's recommended for absolutely everyone, to newcomers and to those familiar with Fullmetal Alchemist.

A lot is always said about FMAB's position as the top place in this site and how it sometimes looks like it's being fiercely maintained in that place artificially. As of me, I don't really believe in aggregated scores or score numbers. I don't think the numbers really tell you that much. I can give something 10/10 and someone else can give it 10/10 but it doesn't in any way mean we have the exact same opinion. That said, when considering the sort of shows that end up rivaling FMAB's position on the list I think there's only few shows like this one that whenI see them listed as "#1 of all time", I can't really say "but," . It's not perfect, there might be better animes out there for the niches you like, but I don't think anyone who thinks this is the best anime of all time is particularly wrong.

Here's a list of things that are very difficult to find in an anime or really in any sort of media. And it's certainly really difficult to find all of these things all at once.

- It's a story worth telling, worth sharing with people. I truly believe that everyone should hear this story.
- The world and its mechanics are interesting, compelling and consistent AND also aren't over-complicated.
- There's a vast variety of characters. You'll love the good guys and the people with more neutral variety and you'll love to hate the villains. And you'll love some of the villains. Everyone has unique ideals and goals in the world.
- Strong theming work. 
- Action anime where the protagonist doesn't have to become increasingly strong and reach a power creep issue.
- Many of the characters mentioned above are women. And they are all incredibly well written characters AND useful for the plot and some are important during the fights AND none of them is a "mary sue" by any stretch of the imagination.
- Romance is not the focus at all, but there are two really compelling couples that I really love to ship and they get tremendous moments.
- The writing is tight. It's clear that the author knew exactly where the story was actually going. Even minor plot happenings have great pay off eventually. 
- It HAS AN ENDING. A proper ending. No stone is left unturned. Characters get their development. Their development gets its pay off. There are no loose ends. Look, when a work is out there trying to claim it's a marsterpiece but also demands forgiveness for having a lackluster ending cause 'endings are hard' , I just think of this show. Endings are hard, but that's what makes good writing and good writers so hard to find. When you find a truly good one, it deserves the praise.
- It gets bleak. It's gets dark. But it also has a positive overall message and its heartwarming and wholesome things.
- Completely flawless set of anime openings and endings that will be part of your playlists forever.
- The fights. are awesome. Plenty of variety in fighting style. "Power level" is never the ultimate thing.

When I got around to watching Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood, I wasn't anticipating quite how compelling and ambitious it would be. From the very first tragic failed human transmutation attempt by the Elric brothers, I was hooked, and the show really didn’t let go until the last episode. The story is epic in scale but also so tightly written, with every subplot, character, and bit of alchemy or Amestris eventually circling back to feed into the grand narrative. The way it transitions between arcs, from Ed and Al's early trials, to the Briggs fortress in the north, to the gargantuan showdown on the Promised Day, makesthe whole thing feel guided and rewarding. Honestly, this has some of the best world-building I’ve ever seen in an anime. Every country, culture, and piece of history adds weight to the story and makes the setting feel alive in a way few series can match.

The characters are what really made this shine for me. Edward and Alphonse carry the series effortlessly. Ed is annoying, stubborn, and hotheaded, but he's also a genius, loyal, and has a solid moral center that makes him impossible not to cheer for. Al is no less compelling, his soft-spoken nature and innocence giving the show its heart. Roy Mustang is also a standout. Funny, driven, and loyal to those he cares for, but there's also a scary edge to him when his cutthroat ambition is unleashed. My overall favorite character was Winry. I loved that she was the emotional glue that kept Ed and Al together, always there to offer a supporting hand, and her passion for automail was just such a cute trait. And then you have characters like Hughes, who brought so much humor and heart, and characters like Scar, who start on one side of the fight but get so much more complex as the show goes on. I could seriously keep going and going because the cast is so vast, but what I really loved is that each and every individual feels memorable and important. The antagonists are also phenomenal. Father and the Homunculi all have their own distinct personalities, and all of them have something terrifying to bring to the table.

On a production level, the series is all but perfect. The animation is consistent throughout, especially during action scenes, where the fights are quick, frantic, and hard-hitting. The soundtrack is lovely and brings out everything from the action-filled fight scenes to the more subdued emotional ones. Voice acting is also superb in both English and Japanese. Romi Park and Rie Kugimiya nail Ed and Al in the sub, and there are great performances across the board in the dub as well. Mustang's Travis Willingham and Hughes's Sonny Strait stood out to me in particular. My only significant gripe was that Ed's English voice made him sound a bit older than he should, but that's a minor quibble in the grand scheme. The pacing does get a bit slow sometimes, but to be honest, it didn't detract from my enjoyment. In the end, I rated Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood 9 out of 10. It's one of the greatest anime experiences I've had, near perfection even, with a phenomenal story, memorable characters, beautiful animation, and a world that will stay with me for a very long time.

Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood — My Review ✨ As someone who entered Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood without reading the original manga or watching the earlier anime adaptation, I approached this series with fresh eyes — and I can confidently say, it exceeded expectations. Airing back in 2009–2010, this anime is over a decade old, and yes — I’m pretty late to the party watching it here in 2025. Coming fresh from watching something modern and polished like Solo Leveling, I was curious if it would still hold up. The answer? Absolutely. The quality, depth, and heart of Brotherhood remain timeless. The journey of Edward and Alphonse Elric is gripping, emotionallylayered, and rich with moral complexity. While the early episodes feel fast-paced — squeezing in a lot of world-building and major plot points — the series soon settles (around episode 15), allowing for deeper character exploration and smoother pacing. The plot is packed with clever twists, philosophical ideas, and tightly linked story threads, all building to a powerful and satisfying conclusion.

The animation is consistently high-quality — crisp visuals, fluid action sequences, and beautifully expressive character designs. The fight scenes are thrilling, making the alchemy battles come alive in every episode. The soundtrack perfectly complements the mood, with memorable openings and endings and an evocative score throughout. Voice acting is excellent across the board, capturing the emotional depth and personality of every character.

One of the greatest strengths of Brotherhood is its outstanding cast. Beyond the Elric brothers, characters like Roy Mustang, Riza Hawkeye, Scar, Ling Yao, and Olivier Armstrong bring richness and complexity to the story. The inclusion of characters from the nation of Xing adds new cultural dimensions, broadening the world in fascinating ways. Best of all, there’s no wasted character here — nearly every hero, villain, and supporting player contributes meaningfully to the plot and character development.

Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is a masterclass in anime storytelling. With no filler, sharp dialogue, and every episode serving the larger narrative, it balances action, humor, heartbreak, and profound themes beautifully. Whether you’re an experienced anime viewer or someone completely new to the genre, this series is a must-watch. Even after all these years, it stands tall as one of the most rewarding anime experiences I’ve had — a true modern classic that stays with you long after the credits roll.

My Rating: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (9/10)

Overview: It's strange that out of the two "Fullmetal Alchemist" anime series, "Brotherhood" is the one with the subtitle, because it should really be the other way round. This is because "Brotherhood" is the anime that faithfully adapts the original manga series written by Hiromu Arakawa, something that very much works in its favour. While the first "Fullmetal Alchemist" was certainly a great anime in its own right, there is much, much more to love about "Brotherhood". This is a better-written, more powerful, action-packed and enjoyable experience from top to bottom, and to call it a masterpiece would be an understatement. Story & World (10/10): No matter whatpowers you may have, some things just can't be done. That's a lesson brothers Edward and Alphonse Elric learn the hard way when they try to resurrect their dead mother using Alchemy, a scientific process that revolves around creating something in exchange for something of equal value. However, resurrecting humans with such a process is regarded as a serious taboo, and for good reason. The experiment proves to be a colossal failure, as not only do they not bring back their mother, but Ed loses an arm and a leg, while Al loses his entire body, forcing Ed to bind his soul to a suit of armour in order to save his life. Now stuck in these forms, Ed and Al embark on a several-year quest to fix their mistake and get back what they lost- not their mother as they planned before, but simply their bodies. Of course, things prove to be far from simple, as not only do they have no idea to find what they need- a Philosopher's Stone, which supposedly has the ability to bend the rules of alchemy- but they soon find themselves in conflict with mysterious demonic beings known as Homunculi, who are plotting something extremely sinister that threatens to reshape the entire world.

While the setting of "Fullmetal Alchemist", the country Amestris, is fictional, it is heavily inspired by early 20th century Britain and Europe. As far as anime go, "Fullmetal Alchemist" is on a whole other level when it comes to world-building, as we end up learning a ton about the country's history dating all the way back to its origins. The concept of Alchemy is explored immensely as well. To be brief, many of the Alchemists are employed by the government as high-ranking officials, and such Alchemists are known as State Alchemists. Edward is one such Alchemist, with Fullmetal Alchemist being his title. What truly separates him from most Alchemists, however, his brother included, is that while most Alchemists need a special symbol called a Transmutation Circle to use Alchemy, for Ed, using it is as simple as clapping his hands together, a power he gained as a result of being confronted by Truth, a supposed God of Alchemy that is believed by many to punish the arrogant. But honestly, as far Alchemy is concerned, I've barely only scratched the surface. When you hear someone say that anything can become anything in this series, they mean it. Throughout the series, you will see Ed, Al and others transmute everything from spears, swords, doors and even fire. It is a concept that is used to its fullest potential, and the series is much deeper and more original because of it.

As incredibly rich as the world-building is, however, the actual storytelling is just as good. While the series starts off very fast-paced, that's only because it's quickly going through things that were already covered in the first anime (with that in mind, I would recommend watching that series, or at least the first half, before you attempt this one). Once all of that is covered, things slow down a good deal to the absolute perfect pace, with things just consistently getting better and better with each passing episode. Everything makes sense, nothing is anti-climactic and things are almost never quite what they initially seem. The themes are plentiful and there are plenty of messages here that are not subtle at all, but absolutely need to be said. Once the series gets its momentum going, it never loses it, and tops off everything with one of the most rewarding, fitting and well-earned endings I have ever seen in any story, anime or not.

Art & Animation (9.5/10):
Even by Studio Bones standards, "Fullmetal Alchemist" is a fantastic-looking series, both for the time it was made and in general. The characters all look distinct and are masterfully drawn, the environments are equally brilliant-looking, the fight scenes are incredibly well-animated and choreographed and the various Alchemy visuals are an absolute joy to behold. There's a little too much deranged animation for my tastes, but this thankfully never distracts too much from the series and, better yet, it appears less and less as the series progresses. In particular, the final quarter of the series features some of the most gorgeous visuals I have ever seen, in animation or otherwise.

Sound & Dialogue (10/10):
There are so many great tracks in "Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood" that it is pretty much impossible to list them all. I honestly don't have a favourite part of the soundtrack for the simple fact that all of it is brilliant. That said, when it comes to particularly noteworthy tracks, the final two openings, "Period" and "Rain" come to mind. The voice acting, however, is even better; Vic Mignogna delivers an incredible performance as Ed that earned him several much-deserved awards, and the series in general boasts one of the finest dub casts ever assembled, including Travis Willingham as Roy Mustang, Maxey Whitehead as Al, Colleen Clinkenbeard as Riza Hawkeye, Caitlin Glass as Winry Rockbell, Monica Rial as May Chang, Todd Haberkorn as Ling Yao, Christopher Sabat as Alex Armstrong and many, many more. Ultimately, just about everything sound-wise is near-flawless, accompanied by a truly fantastic script, and this is just one of many reasons as to why I love this show so much.

Characters (10/10):
Edward Elric is an incredible protagonist, and calling him three-dimensional would honestly be putting it lightly. He starts the series as very immature and short-tempered (particularly in regards to this height) and while this is definitely hilarious, he tones it down a ton over the series, especially when things get very serious towards the end. Even at his worst, though, Ed is shown consistently to be very compassionate and extremely selfless; restoring his brother's body always takes priority over restoring his own and there's never any question that he's becoming what he's fighting against. Hiromu Arakawa could easily have written him as this ruthless person willing to do anything to restore his and his brother's bodies but she didn't and I applaud her for that. After all, part of the brothers' quest is atonement for thinking they could play God, which would be rendered meaningless if they were willing to become monsters. Ed's flaws instead lie in his belief that he can solve all of his problems with Alchemy and, more prominently, his guilt complex, which leads to him initially unwilling to accept help from anyone but Al, and that's largely because they share the same situation. Overtime, however, he learns to accept help from others and to share his burdens, as well as coming to terms with the fact that he is only human, which in turn allows him to forgive himself for his failures. In short, not only is he the single best character this anime has to offer (which is saying a LOT), he's one of the best anime characters ever conceived.

Then there’s Al who is, in many ways, the opposite of his brother. Where Ed is brash, short-tempered and eager for a fight, Al is kind, calm and pacifistic. He also hates to see anybody in pain and will go to great lengths to keep people from dying. However, while it's a lot harder to anger him than his brother, it's not impossible; he doesn't like people claiming it would be cool to have a suit of armour for a body, generally responding to such comments by saying they should be careful what they wish for. After all, while his armoured body does save him and his brother numerous times, it also means he can't eat, sleep or even feel the air around him. As such, he is notably more eager to have his own body restored than Ed is, even keeping a diary of things to eat when he has it back, though his brother's body is ultimately still his main priority. The relationship between the two brothers is bar none the most important one in the series, and actually differs quite a bit from a typical sibling relationship- while most pairs of siblings in fiction tend to have a foolish sibling and a responsible sibling, both Ed and Al have their foolish and responsible moments, which makes them all the more interesting and fleshed-out and helps out their dynamic immensely. As fantastic a character as Al is, however, one who I found myself liking even more is the brothers' commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Roy Mustang. Known as the Flame Alchemist, he has the ability to convert air into flammable gas using a Transmutation Circle on his glove, then lighting a fire to cause a huge burst of flames to attack. He's also a master tactician, deliberately acting much shallower than he actually is so that people don't take him too seriously. Not only is he one of the most badass characters in the series, he's also one of the most idealistic, having grand ambitions for Amestris that will very much benefit the people, in no small part thanks to his strong faith in humanity. These ambitions stem from a desire to make up for a terrible tragedy he took part in in the past, making him come off as a lot like the Elric brothers in this regard, but very different from them at the same time.

Another truly fantastic character is Riza Hawkeye, Roy's second-in-command and closest subordinate who lived through and was forced to do many of the same things he did. She's an incredibly loyal woman who would do anything for Mustang, yet also won't hesitate to remind him of his shortcomings or call him out when he goes too far, generally showing a no-nonsense attitude that hides her warm heart and desire to make up for her past actions, which is justified by the fact that she's a soldier. Plus, as her name implies, she's master marksman, with pretty much all of her best moments coming from her incredible aiming skills. Speaking of great female characters, there's also Winry Rockbell, a childhood friend of Ed and Al as well as the love interest of the former, and a highly skilled mechanic. She doesn't fight, but she still proves to be an invaluable asset to the brothers, both as emotional support and for the fact that she's the one to fix Ed's automail (artificial limbs that he wears in place of the ones he lost) whenever they get broken, which happens quite often, and you can expect her to be pissed whenever it happens. As a bonus, she's a huge geek for machinery, and I'd consider her to be a great character just for that.

As a whole, "Fullmetal Alchemist"'s cast of characters is absolutely mind-boggling. Throughout the anime's 64 episodes, we're introduced to over 100 different characters, and by some miracle, most, if not all of them manage to be important. There's also plenty of strong connections between them, on top of the ones I've already mentioned, which really helps to reinforce the story's many themes. Even you don't like certain characters, you're not meant to. The Homonculi act very much like the sadistic, misanthropic demons they are, but even they all manage to have at least one sympathetic trait. The only real exception is the big boss, and trust me when I say that while you may enjoy the threat he delivers as an antagonist, and the great performance from the voice actor (whom I will not name to avoid spoilers), you will HATE him by the end of the series.

Enjoyment (9.5/10):
"Fullmetal Alchemist" is a massively enjoyable series, having some of the most original fight scenes I've ever seen thanks to the many different uses of Alchemy. There's a ton of great comedy relief as well, whether it be Ed's comical overreactions, Winry's geeking over technology or Ling Yao's trolling among others. The only thing that stops this category from getting full marks is that it takes a bit too long to get to the good stuff, though when it does it will have been absolutely worth the wait, and as I mentioned earlier, things just get better with every episode, meaning you will absolutely want to see it to the end.

Overall:
Even more than a decade after its initial run, "Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood" still stands as an absolute benchmark for all anime, making it hardly a surprise as to why calling it bad or even okay is such a sore spot in the anime community. There isn't a single aspect this series doesn't hit the nail on the head, from its amazingly well-developed characters, its fantastic visuals, its impeccable sound design (the voice acting, in particular), its brilliantly creative fight scenes to its incredible, deep story with a long list of powerful messages that only "Dragon Ball" could hope to match. This is easily one of the greatest shows I have ever seen and comes highly recommended to anyone who is unfortunate enough to have not watched it yet.

Let's make one thing clear before I start this review, I have no experience with the previous incarnation of Fullmetal Alchemist. This series was my first foray into the world of FMA, & I must say, it is VERY excellent. First off, the series has a huge cast of interesting & unique characters. They are each quite different from each other, and act in different ways. The way the series elegantly manages all the character's developments and story lines is a feat in itself. The series also has a fantastically crafted plot, filled with action, humor, & tragedy. Despite its mainstream appeal, it still maintains amature tone that really grabs you.

The animation & art is top notch. You won't be getting any poorly edited sequences or grotesque looking art. The production values are great. I watched the series with the English voice track, and the dub did quite a good job. No complaints there. The soundtrack is excellent as well, particularly the opening & closing sequences that accompany each episode.

It goes on for some 64 episodes, & maintains your attention the entire time. It even manages to close everything up in a satisfying manner. A fantastic series. This show will make you laugh, cry, and even get angry a few times.

Loved it.

The character growth is not only evident in their behavior, but also visually as they literally grow up, which is not something that anime/manga, and especially shonen, usually bothers with outside of timeskips, but in FMA:B, you can see it happening in real time. The characters are all unique, charming, and engaging in their own way, to the point that you could literally just read some lines with no context or voice and you could know who it is, and I'm not just talking about Ed's vendetta against milk. The OPs and ED's are all perfect at their job, which is to communicate the tone and contentof their respective arcs. The first and second ones are more lighthearted with only a little bit of a hint of danger, especially when you know the lyrics, and from there, each new OP becomes more and more serious and dark, until you get to Rain, which is just absolutely flawless in its music and visual elements.
The story itself is also incredible. Usually, you'll get a story that's either character-driven or plot-driven, but this one somehow does both and does it in an incredibly organic way such that you are absolutely 100% invested in what's going on, be it the overall stakes, the emotional growth of the characters, or the action in the moment. The information is drip-fed to us. There's not a single exposition dump anywhere that it couldn't be done fluidly by character interaction. Flashbacks are few and far between and last only long enough to convey what information they need to.
And overall, even as the stakes keep escalating, from the boys to the country to the world, it's still just about the boys getting their bodies back.

And that's why Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood gets a 9/10 and ties for my favorite. It's closer to a 10 than an 8.

“Stand up and walk. Keep moving forward. You've got two good legs. So get up and use them. You're strong enough to make your own path.” FMA Brotherhood tells us the story of two brothers: Edward and Alphonse. They wanted so bad to return their mother's life that they used a forbidden alchemy technique in attempt to bring her back to life. Alchemy is the scientific technique of understanding the structure of matter, decomposing it, and then reconstructing it. It's based on the principle that only one thing can be created from something else of a certain mass: The Principle of Equivalent Exchange. The cost forattempting to revive their mother was losing their bodies parcially or completely. Thas said, the brothers' journey for recovering their bodies using alchemy starts, having plenty of events surrounding it.

So yeah, it's pretty much a shounen anime in essence. However, Hiromu Arakawa (the authoress) revealed a complex plot, with action, comedy and drama all in the measure to bring us a well balanced plot. The story takes place in the Amestris Military State, a country that in the past was the scene of a terrible civil war that almost ended the Ishibalian race. The show is full of conspiracies and terrifying hypotheses involving alchemy and politics, all well tied with extremely captivating characters.

The characters are all great. It's amazing how a show having a large cast was able to handle it with such excellence. Ed and Alphonse stand out as one of the best pairs in shounen with their great strong motives and deeply personal bond. The support cast shines as well. Mustang and Hawkeye relationship is always fun, Scar is a highly intriguing complex villain, Hohenheim with his mysterious background and personality gives is really captivatingt, the Armstrongs are great, so as the teacher. I thought Winry would be the kind of boring useless character, judging by past experience with shounen, but I was pleasantly surprised. Everyone has a purpose, fitting very well into the story.

The anime shows us the various weakness of humankind concerning how we struggle to live inside a society in contrast to our ego and selfish desires. Humans should have a minimum of empathy for things to work out, since even the things we least imagine can be connected. If we become corrupt, it maybe disastrous. We are just humans. We can't live without consequences, as the alchemy's principle states. Plus, it has a meaningful message to take away about the cost of gain and the meaning of perseverance. It's like Ed says:

"A lesson without pain is meaningless. That's because no one can gain without sacrificing something. But by enduring that pain and overcoming it, he shall obtain a powerful, unmatched heart. A fullmetal heart.”

In addition to a fluid animation and a great soundtrack, FMA Brotherhood stands out in every area. I wouldn't say it's perfect though, since the first episode is not a good introduction and the main antagonist should get more attention, but its qualities definitely obfuscates its flaws.

Fullmetal Alchemist Brotherhood is a momentous achievement, not only in the realm of anime, but in the world of fiction as a whole. It is a timeless classic, and should be experienced by all. The story is very complex for a shonen and has so many interlinking and well-developed themes that it almost the ultimate story. The way that Arakawa handles racism, mass genocide, responsibility, death, the cycle of life and the powerof individuals is sublime. So much so, that there are plenty of videos and articles detailing the all of the themes mentioned as well as many more. The only thing that is somewhat disappointing is that Brotherhood specifically rushes through the earlier parts of the story and also has a pretty bad first episode in my opinion.

Characters - Arakawa understands the one most important thing a character needs to seem realistic - flaws. Each and every character in the series, whether good or evil, has a flaw in some way. From Van Hohenheim's insecurities with his immortality and his family, to Ed's rash and somewhat immature attitude to the events around him, to Fuhrer King Bradley's hypocritical view on the importance of humanity. All of these imperfections not only create clear and satisfying character development, but also allows the viewer to sympathize with them. Another thing that I like is that there are some morally grey characters too. Take Scar, for example, who doesn't necessarily ever repent the actions he's committed, even though they are objectively bad.

Art - This is FMA:B's most unimpressive aspect, at face value at least. The art is very clean and consistent but doesn't try to go too stylized. However, Arakawa's artwork shines due to how malleable it is to the current emotion trying to be portrayed. It is just disproportional enough for the comedic moments but also beautiful enough for the more serious moments.

Sound - As far as the OPs go, they are all pretty great, especially "Again" and "Period". The soundtrack in the anime itself is also quite good. It's very bombastic and atmospheric, but I do honestly prefer the marvel that was the soundtrack to FMA 2003. The voice acting in both sub and dub is exceptional, and, let's be honest, even the most die-hard dub haters will agree FMA:B's English dub is very, very good. 

Overall - Honestly, this review is kind of pointless. Everyone who is in the anime community already knows about FMA:B's legacy. After all, it is the single highest rated anime series on this site. so don't take my word for it. Take the anime community's word for it and watch Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood.

Disclaimer: This review is not about comparing Brotherhood to its predecessor from 2003 or the manga. I am reviewing this show as a stand-alone series. It is no secret that Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is popular. FMA: Brotherhood still gets overwhelmingly positive feedback from the anime community, although it finished airing over ten years ago. However, being a popular show does not always mean that it is good. That is why one of the most remarkable things to note about Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is how it is recognized and acknowledged by the community. It is either included in hundreds of ‘The best anime of all time’ listsall over the internet or ranked by thousands of people as the best show on several platforms, specifically on AniList, MyAnimeList, and Anime News Network. What makes it so special? What does Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood have that the other similar shows lack? Why do thousands of people all over the world love it? So, in an attempt to answer those questions, let’s dissect the show and figure out together why this title is so heart-warming yet bitter-sweet and overall fantastic and amusing shounen. Although this anime might not need an introduction, I’ll still start with the basics for the people who have never heard about FMA or are not familiar with the series.

Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is definitely one of the top-notch shows because of how it explores and builds the world of its universe.
Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is the second anime adaptation of Fullmetal Alchemist manga written by Hiromu Arakawa. The show first aired in April 2009 and continued its run until July 2010, finishing with 64 episodes in total. It was developed by the studio Bones that gave us such popular titles as Ouran High School Host Club, Soul Eater, Noragami, MHA, and many other decent series. The remake of the 2003 anime is known for following the manga as close as a show can. That is why the fans fell in love with the Brotherhood even more since there are only two filler and four mixed cannon episodes out of 64.

In the world of Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood, alchemy plays a crucial role in multiple major aspects of the show, including its most basic plot. Alchemy is presented to us as this ancient scientific abstract art of manipulation and alteration of matter by using natural energy. What alchemy essentially does, it comprehends, deconstructs, and reconstructs. While this technique sounds amazing, there is one golden rule, the basis of all alchemy, "In order for something to be obtained, something of equal value must be lost". Our two protagonists, young Elric brothers, Edward being the oldest and Alphonse being the youngest, learned this Law of Equivalent Exchange the hard way after attempting human transmutation, the taboo of all alchemists. As a result of the violation, the older brother loses his left leg, while the younger one his body. Scared of his brother being completely taken away from him, Edward sacrifices his right arm to attach Alphonse’s soul to a suit of armor. Now, their main goal is to return to their normal, human selves, since Alphonse is now connected to a huge body armor suit and Edward gets mechanical replacements, automail, for his missing limbs and becomes a state alchemist carrying the name Fullmetal Alchemist. As mentioned above, this is the fundamental plot of the series. Now, what makes FMA: Brotherhood such an incredible anime is not how multidimensional the show is but how multilayered it is. While on a 3-year-long dangerous adventure to return their original bodies, the Elric brothers discover the existence of a powerful artifact called the Philosopher's Stone, which allows alchemists to overcome and ‘break’ the above stated Law of Equivalent Exchange. In return for learning about the Stone (yes, I just referenced the Law), Edward and Alphonse learn the shady story of their own country by getting caught in a governmental conspiracy while uncovering the real nature of the Philosopher's Stone.

As you can see, the bedrock of this show is quite diverse and includes a bunch of food for thought starting from something as basic as the significance of family relationships and ending with a dreadful question about what makes one human. However, the most crucial aspect that separates FMA from many other shounen anime, in my opinion, is the existence of the Law in the show’s universe. I noticed that a lot of shounens nowadays fail to set up any ground rules, which leads to complete absurdity, overpowered characters, and nonsensical tropes. It was nice to see Fullmetal Alchemist lay out the basic principle of its universe for the viewers and stick to it, instead of coming up with random explanations and ‘breakthroughs’ on the fly just for the sake of amusing the audience.

I strongly believe that the overall plot of this anime is incredibly interesting, starting from the brothers’ desire to have human bodies again and ending on the discourse about the military conspiracy that is rooted so deep into Amestris, the country where the action happens. In my eyes, even if we put aside characters, their development, and other aspects aside, it is safe to say that FMA is definitely one of the top-notch anime because of how it explores and builds the world of its universe, how it unpacks all of the enigmas through tiny details not only in dialogs or flashbacks but the animation itself, how it makes you, the viewer, question what is good, what is evil, or do these definitions even exist. Clearly, there are so many moments where you feel so happy for the ‘good’ characters in the show but what makes Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood a part of an amazing-anime-club is how it creates the connection between the viewer and the ‘bad guys’. Speaking in a bit of a harsh and general manner for the sake of avoiding spoilers, the show plays with your feelings to a certain degree and makes you wonder if the villains deserve the punishment or not.

Fullmetal Alchemist might seem to be kinda fast-paced at times but it makes up for it by staying consistent, regardless of the speed at which we are being told a story about two brothers, their family, friends, and comrades. It might seem like we are moving really fast at a certain point because the show tries to unpack a million different topics in a very short period of time, sometimes it’s reversed. However, it is essential to remember, everything that happens on the screen happens for a reason. As mentioned above, this anime has little to no fillers but even those are tied to the story smartly. Therefore, if the event seems to have no meaning behind it or it feels rushed, my advice would be: trust the process; it will all make sense in the end.

FMA: Brotherhood is a shounen after all, so you get a lot of breaks from or during serious moments when staff decides to input some funny animation or dialog to kindly remind us to have fun while watching the show instead of constantly being focused on the seriousness of it. From my perspective, it is a nice touch to the anime because at the end of the day it is an entertainment medium. I see FMA get criticism for inserting banters because they ‘don’t fit the mood of the scene’, however, I personally disagree with that. FMA can get very intense at times and those funny moments are used in really clever ways to reduce our, the viewers, tension.

I dare to say that FMA has slim to no one-dimensional characters.
I’ve briefly mentioned some characters’ aspects above, so I’m going to dive deeper into characters and their ‘quality’ in this section, which is a quite difficult topic to dissect. It is difficult mainly because this show creates a narrative where it plays with your head, emotions, and rationale, making you believe that nearly every character is the main character of the show. I know, it sounds a bit strange and overwhelming but FMA does it in such a shrewd manner where you don’t really notice that you care so much about this specific side character and actually treat it as the main one for a second. The show usually achieves this effect by, for example, giving you their backstory, analyzing (in a way) someone’s dialog, manners, values through other characters. Obviously, the majority of the screen and storytime goes to the Elric brothers but it would be inexcusable to not mention how well this show treats its side characters, how much love goes into them (both good and bad guys). Each character has a personality, there are no clones in the interest of adding some extra faces to the cast. Although there is a somewhat clear separation between what the good and the bad guys want and need, it can be said with confidence, there are little to no characters that lack some sort of identity. Some of the cast wants to return to their original bodies, others want to rule the country, others want to restore their family’s honor. Therefore, I dare to say that FMA has slim to no one-dimensional characters.

Much like the plot, now and then it might seem as if there are a lot of characters in the show but they are all there for a reason. From my standpoint, Fullmetal Alchemist is the anime where the side characters build up the main ones, the Elric brothers, and intensify the plot. I think that this is something you rarely see in the shounens nowadays because the main character(s) is/are expected to carry the weight of the show, while FMA in some sense splits the story baggage and puts it on everyone included in the show. By doing so, the series can explore multiple characters without really overwhelming the viewers because (almost) every single one of them has some significance to the show that they carry, subtle or not. Therefore, Fullmetal Alchemist gives us so many characters to choose from that we might be able to relate to and connect with on a deeper level. Not only that but, in some cases, it makes our empathy for not-so-good-but-also-not-really-evil characters to get through and questions our own humanity through the Elric brothers’ eyes.

While we are talking about subtleties, this show has a huge number of small, tiny details that bear immeasurable value that is hidden not only in physical objects in that universe (actually drawing/animation wise) but in the personalities, specifically in regards to villains. Those little elements don’t really affect the plot that much since it is not a big deal if you don’t notice them. However, this is why FMA: Brotherhood has such massive rewatchable potential. Trust me, after rewatching the show at least once, you will notice something that you never observed. Although this show doesn’t disappoint you, has a well-written ending and everything falls into place, there still will be a moment in your head when everything just falls into place even more after you rewatch at least the second half of the show. It feels incredibly empowering (in a way) when you realize and detect certain tiny things in the show. It makes us, the viewers, feel like we have truly emerged into that universe and are a part of it. It allows us to continue creating and building that universe in our heads. That is what makes this show an incredible piece of work.

Some words about animation and soundtrack (I suck at this part).
I am personally not a very artistic person and I prefer to focus on other things about the show, so it’s somewhat difficult to talk about animation or music. However, one of the things I would love to say is that FMA’s animation aged very well. While I was watching it, it was really hard to believe that this anime was done in 2009. There were multiple scenes throughout the series that I am pretty sure were money-shots. The color palettes follow the ‘mood’ of the series, the timeline is set in as well as the atmosphere of different scenes. I really enjoyed watching the fighting scenes since they were not as obnoxious to the eye as other shounens scenes nowadays (I’m blind as a bat and sensitive to light because of chronic headaches).

Soundtracks, openings, and endings were incredible, although some of the openings were inconsistent in their structure (when they introduced characters) and animation (coloring wise) but the animation itself saved those ones. The music fits perfectly (to my tastes) and doesn’t feel disconnected from the show. My most favorite part about this show is when they insert the ending song when something really important starts to happen, and then it is slowly transitioned into the regular ending animation sequence.

TL;DR
The bedrock of this show is quite diverse and includes a bunch of food for thought starting from something as basic as the significance of family relationships and ending with a dreadful question about what makes one human. In my eyes, even if we put aside characters, their development, and other aspects aside, it is safe to say that FMA is definitely one of the top-notch anime because of how it explores and builds the world of that universe, how it unpacks all of the enigmas through tiny details not only in dialogs or flashbacks but the animation itself, how it makes you, the viewer, question what is good, what is evil, or do these definitions even exist.

Each character has a personality, there are no clones in the interest of adding some extra faces to the cast. Although there is a somewhat clear separation between what the good and the bad guys want and need, it can be said with confidence, there are little to no characters that lack some sort of identity. Therefore, Fullmetal Alchemist gives us so many characters to choose from that we might be able to relate to and connect with on a deeper level. Not only that but, in some cases, it makes our empathy for not-so-good-but-also-not-really-evil characters to get through and questions our own humanity through the Elric brothers’ eyes.

FMA’s animation aged very well. The music fits perfectly and doesn’t feel disconnected from the show.

Well now. I've now seen this one. I don't know if there's anything I can say that hasn't already been said much better by other people, but here we go. Pros: - Probably the greatest story ever told in anime. The calmer moments, the action scenes, and even the backstory moments do nothing except aid the story resulting in one of the greatest climaxes and conclusions I've seen maybe ever. - Amazingly fleshed out characters which the audience is able to relate with you watch them on this massive, epic, journey. - Villains are written great as unlike a lot of shows/movies/etc. they pose an actualthreat.  There are no OP protagonists here.  Each character is given very believable strengths and weakness that make the action scenes that much more entertaining and awesome.

- Japanese voice actors do a flawless job for these characters (especially Edward).

- Soundtrack is great.  It feels very cinematic and huge which is perfect for this anime which also feels very cinematic and huge.

- Animation looks quite good also.  The final 10 or 15 episodes especially stand out in my memory as having very good art and animation quality.

- Some interesting ideas thrown around regarding the place and purpose of government in society.  There's actually quite intelligent commentary throughout about how a country can disservice it's people simply by being overpowered and lacking transparency and mutual trust with its citizens.

- Without giving anything away (although I'm sure most of you know by now what I'm referring to) Thanks a lot episode 4, you now have the distinction of being the first anime episode that was so screwed up that I had to take a break from this series altogether.

Cons:

- Not really a legitimate criticism, but this series suffers from a serious case of sakuga.

- While I do think such a grand-scaled story deserved to have tons of characters in it, I do think that maybe there were possibly a bit too many characters (mostly minor ones).  Often there'd be characters that were introduced in a couple episodes and served a purpose for that arc, and then about 20 or 30 episodes later they'd show up out of the blue after I'd forgotten about what purpose they served earlier.  Kind of a minor nitpick, and one that's mostly due to the fact that midway I took an extended break from it, but I still think it is something that needs addressing.

Overview:

The best way I can describe this anime is that it's sort of like a Japanese, steampunk version of Lord Of The Rings.  Similar to Lord Of The Rings it is a massive story that needs to be visited at least once in your life.  So much goes on throughout the course of this 64 episode series that the only way they could have done it true justice is by adding 64 more episodes.  For what we got, though, it still manages to captivate the audience and engage it in the journey of these heroes whose quest descends deeper and deeper into hidden, undesired, truths taking their journey in many different directions.  This is truly one of the most fascinating epics I've encountered, and I highly recommend it if you are looking for a fantastic fantasy adventure that is intelligent and adult it nature while also being very accessible and not overwhelmingly complex.  An absolute recommendation.  See it now if you haven't already.
